items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Drug Delivery System Design: From Predictive Modeling to Inverse Formulation Design
items.abstract: AI is revolutionising medication delivery research by enabling data-driven prediction, multidimensional formulation optimisation and rational design of delivery devices with increased therapeutic performance. Traditional drug delivery development is heavily dependent on iterative experimental approaches, empirical manipulation of formulations and step-wise optimisation of single formulation variables which are resource intensive and potentially inadequate to capture complex non-linear interactions between drugs, excipients, physicochemical characteristics, biological barriers and process parameters. Machine learning, deep learning, artificial neural networks and AI-based generative computational techniques offer possibilities to model these multidimensional interactions and to speed up the finding of formulations with defined performance features. Predictive modelling can be used to predict drug release kinetics, physico-chemical stability, pharmacokinetic behaviour, drug-excipient compatibility and carrier related properties to support early stage formulation decisions. AI-assisted optimisation enables systematic combination of formulation and process parameters to identify parameter combinations that result in good drug loading capacity, particle properties, encapsulation efficiency, stability and controlled or targeted release. More recently, a new paradigm was developed called inverse design approaches where the desired therapeutic/material features are first described and mathematical models then propose potential formulations that can achieve the predefined characteristics. Coupling generative AI with inverse design could further boost this capacity to build novel delivery structures outside the empirically investigated formulation space. However, there remain several challenges to be addressed, including data heterogeneity, limited datasets, model interpretability, external validation, reproducibility, regulatory approval, and the translation of computational predictions to clinically viable formulations. This review critically discusses the evolving role of AI in drug delivery with focus on forecasting, formulation optimisation and emerging inverse design strategies as well as translational barriers and future opportunities to develop more efficient, personalised and rationally engineered systems for drug delivery.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Education: Rethinking Curriculum, Assessment, and the Role of the Teacher
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how learners access information, practise skills, receive feedback, and demonstrate understanding. These developments create an opportunity to reconsider curricula that place disproportionate emphasis on recall, but they do not make foundational knowledge or memorisation obsolete. This perspective article argues that schools should integrate AI as a means of strengthening inquiry, critical evaluation, creativity, problem-solving, and ethical judgement while preserving the human relationships and disciplinary knowledge on which learning depends. Drawing on selected literature and a practitioner reflection from an international-school context in Angola, the article proposes a curriculum-oriented approach organised around four connected priorities: competency-focused learning objectives, assessment redesign, educator development, and explicit AI literacy. It also considers risks involving unequal access, unreliable outputs, privacy, bias, academic integrity, and over-reliance. The school-based reflection is presented as an illustrative account rather than a formal evaluation, because systematic outcome data are not reported. The article concludes with practical recommendations for school leaders, teachers, policymakers, and accreditation bodies. Responsible integration requires more than access to tools: it requires clear governance, equitable provision, informed professional judgement, and assessment practices that make students’ thinking visible.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN ENGLISH LANGUAGE TEACHING AND INNOVATIVE APPROACHES IN LEARNING
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is becoming one of the most important innovations in modern education, and its role in English language teaching is growing rapidly. In recent years, AI-based tools such as chatbots, automated writing assistants, speech-recognition programs, and adaptive learning platforms have changed the way students learn English. These technologies provide new opportunities for practising language skills, receiving immediate feedback, and organising independent learning. As a result, English language teaching is gradually moving from traditional teacher-centred instruction toward more flexible and learner-centred models.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Mental Health Referral and Documentation: An Analysis of Clinician Reflections
items.abstract: Abstract As artificial intelligence (AI) and automation become embedded across the continuum of mental health care, their influence is increasingly felt not only in therapeutic encounters but in the infrastructural processes that surround them. Aim This paper explores how technology-based referral platforms and AI-assisted documentation address two major barriers to care: delays in access and the stigma of seeking mental health or substance use services. Method This study employed a qualitative, exploratory design to examine how clinicians perceive and respond to artificial intelligence (AI) assisted referral and documentation tools within mental health and social work practice. Results Analysis of practitioner reflections revealed three overarching themes: 1) perceived benefits and workflow improvements, 2) ethical ambivalence and concerns around consent, and 3) clinical identity and resistance to automation. The themes illustrate the complex landscape clinicians navigate when adopting AI-based documentation tools. Conclusion Clinicians’ reflections on AI are not merely technical. They are deeply tied to questions of professional identity, relational ethics, and the nature of evidence-based practice. This study highlights the need to reframe AI not as a replacement for clinical reasoning or narrative complexity but as a potential ally, one that must be thoughtfully designed and governed.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Public Administration: Delegation of Functions, Responsibility, and Legitimation Practices
items.abstract: The article examines the process of the artificial intelligence (AI) systems implementation into the structures of public administration focusing on the actual distribution of the powers of authority, the problem of accountabil-ity, and discursive legitimation practices. Based on a qualitative comparative analysis of four international cas-es (Romania, China, the USA, the UK), it is established that the AI systems primarily perform information pro-cessing functions and routing tasks, without replacing a human at the stage of final political decision-making. The study proves that the public presentation of the AI is often used by authorities as a legitimation tool to demonstrate competence, impartiality, and technological modernity even when the actual role of the algorithm is limited. It is concluded that the prospects of total algocracy do not yet give cause for concern as the AI activity is still incorporated in the current mechanisms of power and serves only to renew officials’ institutional reputa-tion.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN RECRUITMENT: EFFECTIVENESS, RISKS AND ETHICAL LIMITATIONS
items.abstract: The article examines the effectiveness, risks, and ethical limitations of artificial intelligence (AI) in recruitment. A distinction is made between deterministic automation, algorithmic systems, machine learning, and generative AI, which makes it possible to avoid equating any digital HR tool with artificial intelligence. Based on a systematized review of recent academic literature, comparative and content analysis, as well as analysis of regulatory documents, the evidence regarding the impact of AI on recruitment performance is synthesized. It is shown that the strongest evidence concerns operational effects: the ability to process large volumes of applications, automate repetitive tasks, support sourcing, screening, matching, and communication, and reduce recruiters’ workload. At the same time, the evidence is substantially less conclusive with respect to quality of hire, candidate experience, and the elimination of bias. The article analyzes algorithmic bias, indirect discrimination, opacity, false exclusion of qualified candidates, privacy and information-security risks, automation bias, and the potential dehumanization of recruitment. Particular attention is paid to meaningful human oversight and to the current regulatory framework, including the EU AI Act, the GDPR, and Ukrainian legislation. An author-developed matrix for assessing the appropriateness of AI use in recruitment is proposed. It combines the expected effect, strength of evidence, discrimination and privacy risks, severity of potential error, and the required level of human oversight. Three modes of AI use are substantiated: automation-preferred, AI-assisted decision-making, and human-led decision-making. The principle of proportionality between automation and risk is formulated, according to which the permissible autonomy of an AI system should decrease as the potential harm of an algorithmic outcome increases.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Sport: Applications, Evidence, Limitations, and Directions for Responsible Implementation
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in sport through machine learning, computer vision, wearable sensing, predictive modelling, and automated analytics. This narrative review synthesizes evidence on AI applications in athlete performance analysis, movement recognition, training support, injury-risk modelling, return-to-sport decision support, talent identification, tactical analysis, officiating, and fan-facing systems. Foundational reviews demonstrate substantial research activity: a 2019 review identified 58 studies across 12 team sports and a pooled sample of 6,456 participants, while a systematic review of sport-specific movement recognition included 52 studies. More recent evidence shows rapid growth in injury prediction research but also persistent methodological limitations. A 2025 scoping review included 38 injury-risk studies and reported that tree-based approaches achieved the highest statistical performance in 60% of studies; however, small datasets and heterogeneous injury definitions limited clinical utility. A 2026 systematic review of 18 empirical injury-prediction studies found that only one study (5.6%) had low overall risk of bias, with external validation remaining uncommon. Collectively, the literature supports AI as a promising decision-support technology rather than an autonomous replacement for coaches, clinicians, sports scientists, or officials. Future work should prioritize external validation, representative athlete cohorts, transparent reporting, explainability, privacy protection, and prospective evaluation in real-world sporting environments.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in Vehicular Ad Hoc Networks a systematic review of applications challenges and future directions
items.abstract: Vehicular Ad Hoc Networks (VANETs) are an important component of Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS), enabling real-time communication to support road safety, mobility, and transportation efficiency. However, dynamic network topology, stringent latency requirements, security and privacy threats, communication overhead, and resource constraints continue to challenge reliable vehicular communication. Artificial Intelligence (AI) provides data-driven approaches for intelligent routing, adaptive communication, intrusion detection, predictive maintenance, and distributed decision-making. This paper presents a systematic literature review of AI applications in VANETs covering studies published from January 2018 to 30 June 2026. Following the PRISMA 2020 methodology, the literature is organized into four themes: AI-based routing and communication optimization, security and privacy enhancement, predictive maintenance and vehicle health monitoring, and emerging AI paradigms for intelligent vehicular networking. The review compares AI techniques, datasets, communication technologies, evaluation environments, performance metrics, and reported limitations. The synthesis highlights the growing adoption of Reinforcement Learning, Deep Learning, Federated Learning, Graph Neural Networks, and Edge Intelligence across these domains. Key challenges include data heterogeneity, dynamic environments, scalability, communication overhead, privacy, explainability, resource constraints, and reproducibility. Future directions include federated edge intelligence, dynamic graph learning, AI-native 6G, semantic communication, Digital Twins, multimodal AI, and trustworthy AI for scalable and secure vehicular networks.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE INTEGRATION AND ACADEMIC PERFORMANCE IN PHILIPPINE SECONDARY EDUCATION: A MIXED-METHODS STUDY OF ICT LITERACY AND CLASSROOM CHALLENGES
items.abstract: This study examined artificial intelligence (AI) utilization, associated classroom challenges, and academic performance among Senior High School students at Tigao National High School, Surigao del Sur, Philippines, during the Academic Year 2025-2026. Employing a mixed-methods research design, the study involved 122 respondents comprising 107 students and 15 teachers. Quantitative data were gathered through questionnaires and pretest–posttest assessments and analyzed using descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, and paired-samples t-tests, while qualitative data were examined through thematic analysis. Findings revealed that respondents demonstrated functional ICT literacy (M = 3.72) and frequently utilized AI for research, writing assistance, and academic activities. Academic performance increased from a pretest mean percentage score of 60.76% to 65.42% in written assessments and 79.53% in oral assessments, with statistically significant differences (p < .05). ICT literacy demonstrated a significant positive relationship with academic performance (r = .52, p < .05). Qualitative findings identified unreliable internet connectivity, limited devices, academic integrity concerns, and excessive AI dependence as persistent challenges. The study concluded that responsible AI integration, strengthened digital literacy, and appropriate instructional safeguards are essential to supporting academic achievement and equitable technology-enhanced learning.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Integration in the Documentation and Revitalisation of African Oral Traditions: Challenges and Prospects
items.abstract: Rationale of the Study – This study examines the challenges and prospects of integrating Artificial Intelligence into the documentation and revitalisation of African oral traditions. Methodology – The study employed a qualitative research approach within an interpretivist paradigm. It explores the potential role of artificial intelligence in documenting and revitalising African oral traditions. It employs a conceptual review and analytical synthesis, building its arguments from existing literature in technology, history, culture, and the Technology Acceptance Model. The study analysed data from secondary sources using content analysis. Findings – Preserving oral traditions in Africa faces several challenges, as it depends on people's past activities and experiences. Compared with humans, Artificial Intelligence (AI) can store large amounts of information in both tangible and intangible formats, providing access for current and future generations. The study identified several challenges to AI adoption, including high installation costs, inadequate skills among archivists, ethical concerns about data privacy and user security, and insufficient training on AI use. Implications – The study recommended the formulation of well-written AI use policies, training for archivists on ethical use of AI, and encouraged elders to share their knowledge with the archivists to ensure such knowledge is captured by the AI for long-term use. Originality – The originality lies in using a qualitative research approach and the Technology Acceptance Model, which provides an in-depth understanding of AI use in documenting and revitalising African oral traditions.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Literacy and Public Acceptance of AI Technologies among Adults in Iraq
items.abstract: This study investigated the relationship between Artificial Intelligence (AI) literacy and public acceptance of AI technologies among adults in Iraq. The role of AI in public services, healthcare, education, banking, and digital communication is growing, making it a key sociological and policy issue to understand what factors affect citizens' acceptance of AI. A quantitative cross sectional survey design was used and data were gathered from 420 adults living in Iraq. Artificial Intelligence literacy and public acceptance of AI technologies were measured by a structured questionnaire with a five-point Likert scale. The data were analysed by descriptive statistics, Cronbach's alpha, exploratory factor analysis, Pearson correlation and regression analysis using IBM SPSS Statistics software. The results showed that the participants had a moderate to high level of AI literacy and moderate levels of public acceptance of AI technologies. The Pearson correlation analysis showed that there was a statistically significant positive correlation between the concepts of artificial intelligence literacy and public acceptance. The regression analysis also revealed that AI literacy was a significant predictor of public acceptance, accounting for 32.0% of the variance, and multiple regression analysis indicated that AI literacy is the most significant predictor, even after controlling for demographic and technology-related characteristics. The study is a significant contribution to the sociology of artificial intelligence, as it illustrates how AI literacy is a crucial social resource that influences citizens' receptivity to new technologies. The results highlight the need to encourage AI literacy initiatives to foster informed public acceptance and facilitate responsible digital transformation in Iraq.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Models for Breast Cancer Prediction: A Comprehensive Review
items.abstract: Breast cancer (BC) caused death in the worldwide, which raises the issue of the urgent essential for accurate and primary prediction. In oncology, we are seeing the rapid integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI), inclusive machine learning and deep learning, and we view this as a transformative opportunity to improve predictive analytics. This review paper looks at the present state of artificial intelligence (AI) in the prediction of breast cancer, which is the most common of all the malignancies worldwide. We examine the synthesis and analysis of recent advances, methods, and performance results for many AI models, inclusive ML and DL models. DL architectures, in particular Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), have achieved the best results in image-based detection tasks. Furthermore, the paper highlights that what may be the here and now in terms of performance does not diminish the value and interpretability of traditional ML models used for structured clinical and genomic data.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Technologies In Digital Radio Broadcasting: Content Creation, Audience Analysis, And Automation Of Broadcasting Processes
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of digital technologies has produced fundamental transformations in the media system, and radio broadcasting in particular. The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies into broadcasting practice is redefining how content is prepared, edited, distributed, and used to engage audiences. Employing a qualitative literature review and conceptual-theoretical analysis, this study systematically examines the principal domains in which AI is applied to radio broadcasting: automated news-text generation, speech synthesis, music and content personalization, audience-behavior analytics, and broadcast-process automation. The research situates these developments within an interdisciplinary theoretical framework informed by McLuhan’s medium theory, Rogers’s diffusion of innovations, Diakopoulos’s concept of algorithmic hybridization, Katz and Blumler’s uses-and-gratifications approach, and Habermas’s notion of the public sphere. Comparative case material is drawn from RadioGPT in the United States, the bigGPT project on Germany’s bigFM, will.i.am’s RAiDiO.FYI platform, and the Australian station CADA’s AI host “Thy,” alongside a localized assessment of Azerbaijan’s media landscape through ASAN TV’s virtual presenter Asaniyya. The findings indicate that AI enhances production efficiency, optimizes resource allocation, and enables personalized content delivery, while simultaneously raising unresolved ethical and legal questions concerning transparency, copyright, data privacy, algorithmic bias, and the future of the journalistic profession. The study concludes that a hybrid broadcasting model, grounded in the complementarity of human creativity and machine capability, represents the most sustainable trajectory for the future of radio.

items.title: Artificial intelligence-enabled acceleration and enhancement of 4D device printing
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are rapidly emerging as necessary computational paradigms for 4D device printing—the additive manufacturing of structures programmed to dynamically transform their shape, properties, or functions over time in response to external stimuli. Unlike standard 3D printing, which targets static geometric fidelity and steady-state structural properties, 4D printing involves solving a highly non-linear, path-dependent inverse problem across coupled material-geometry-process-stimulus spaces. This commentary presents the central argument that data-driven and physics-informed AI methods are not merely optional optimizations, but mandatory tools required to navigate the temporal multi-physics design space and make 4D printing deterministic, reproducible, and commercially viable. We clearly delineate between methods already empirically demonstrated (e.g., forward surrogate neural networks, convolutional inverse design of metamaterials, active learning for material discovery, and melt-pool defect detection) and methods currently proposed (e.g., autonomous closed-loop digital twins, physics-informed neural ODEs for long-term degradation, and certified explainable AI pipelines for clinical implants). Furthermore, we distinguish the evidence base for static 3D printing (focusing on relative density, void formation, and static residual stresses) from dynamic 4D printing (focusing on spatiotemporal deformation, phase transformation kinetics in shape-memory alloys, rate-dependent hydrogel swelling, and hysteresis). We highlight the unique challenges of 4D printing—specifically, non-linear multi-physics coupling, extreme computational cost, sparse spatiotemporal experimental data, inverse design non-uniqueness, and actuation drift—and demonstrate qualitatively how physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), active learning, deep generative models, and computer-vision digital twins solve these bottlenecks. Finally, we re-emphasize in our conclusion the transformative role of spatiotemporal AI in bridging lab-scale smart materials and production-grade 4D functional systems.

items.title: Artificial intelligence-enabled updating and application of guideline-based algorithms for symptom management in adults with cancer: a concordance evaluation of cancer-related fatigue, depression, and pain
items.abstract: Introduction Cancer-related fatigue, depression, and pain are highly prevalent, often co-occur and impair physical function, social activities, and quality of life among adults with cancer. Despite the availability of evidence-based clinical guidelines that provide recommendations for assessment and management, these symptoms remain under-recognized and undertreated. Clinical decision support systems (CDSS) can operationalize guideline-based symptom management algorithms at the point of care. However, maintaining these systems as evidence and practice evolve is labor-intensive, limiting adoption and sustainability. To address this gap, we sought to evaluate an artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled approach to updating guideline-based algorithms and generating patient-specific recommendations for managing fatigue, depression, and pain among adults with cancer. Methods This study evaluated AI performance (Gemini 3.0 Pro) for two tasks: identifying and interpreting updates to cancer symptom management guidelines for fatigue, depression, and pain, and producing casespecific recommendations aligned with an existing rule-based CDSS. Guideline updates were assessed against expert-judged reference standards using an ordinal rubric for detection, completeness, accuracy, and safety. Vignette-based recommendations were compared using precision, recall, and F1-score at the level of discrete clinical recommendation elements. Results For guideline updating, AI performance met pre-specified acceptability thresholds for fatigue and pain, with high completeness and accuracy and no clinical safety risk. Performance for depression was variable, driven by omission of guideline-supported integrative therapies and non-specific pharmacotherapy guidance. In vignette analyses, AI-generated recommendations showed strong concordance with the rule-based CDSS (F1 0.86–0.96). Most mismatches between AI and the CDSS came from AI leaving something out, not from giving unsafe advice. Discussion This suggests AI currently works best as a support tool rather than making clinical decisions on its own. Broader clinical use will require further work to test a greater number of test vignettes and its performance in real-world, multi-site settings with diverse patient populations.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence‐Based Smart Gold Mining Site Status Classification Using Deep Learning
items.abstract: ABSTRACT The increasing adoption of digital technologies in mining generates large volumes of operational data that can support intelligent monitoring and decision‐making. However, accurately determining whether a gold mining site is active or inactive remains challenging because mining operations involve multiple interrelated operational, workforce, energy, and production factors. This study proposes the Artificial Intelligence‐Based Smart Gold Mining Site Status Classification Using Deep Learning (AISME‐DLOAR) framework for automated classification of gold mining sites into Active and Inactive categories. The proposed framework consists of data preprocessing, hybrid wrapper‐based feature selection using Boruta and Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE), and a Graph Convolutional Neural Network integrated with Multi‐Head Attention (GCNN‐MHA). In the graph representation, each mining‐site record is treated as a node, while similarity relationships among mining sites are represented as edges, enabling the model to learn both feature characteristics and relationships among related sites. AdamW optimization is employed to improve training stability and generalization. Experiments on the Traditional Gold Mining in Sudan dataset containing 22,398 records demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves 98.52% accuracy, 98.60% precision, 98.52% recall, 98.56% F1‐score, and 97.12% MCC on the 70:30 testing configuration. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of AISME‐DLOAR for intelligent gold mining‐site status classification and operational monitoring.

items.title: Assessing and developing sector HFE readiness. A transport case study
items.abstract: The adoption of human factors and ergonomics (HFE) as a discipline and the perspectives, methods, and work that flows from it is highly variable across disciplines, and compared with overseas, very few New Zealand sectors have HFE embedded into their day-to-day ways of working. Arguably aviation and rail are the greatest users of HFE, and there is emerging adoption in sectors such as healthcare and the land transport sectors. As part of the earlier workforce development initiative a Needs Assessment Tool was developed and tested. The tool allows assessment of the maturity of various dimensions of organisational work where HFE typically has an influence. Within the Land Transport sector, a short course was developed Human Factors and Ergonomics within the Land Transport System, which was very well received based on a post course participant survey. Various HFE qualified individuals also hold positions within organisations, but not all carry out HFE work within their roles. Using the land transport sector as a case study, this presentation will summarise the existing HFE readiness within the land transport sector and highlight areas of progress and ongoing challenge. A discussion is invited for a broader discussion of HFE adoption in New Zealand based on experiences in other domains, and what further effort is needed to embed HFE into appropriate sectors.

items.title: Assessment of Particulate Matter Emissions from Corn-Milling Sites in Cape Coast Metropolitan, Southern Ghana
items.abstract: Abstract Food milling operations in informal urban markets of Sub-Saharan Africa generate substantial particulate matter (PM) emissions, yet longitudinal, size-resolved data on PM dynamics and associated occupational health risks remain scarce for Ghanaians. A 10-month longitudinal observational study (March–December 2024) was conducted at two commercial milling markets in Cape Coast, Ghana: Kotokoroba and Kingsway. IQAir AirVisual Outdoor monitors deployed at breathing height (1.5 m) recorded PM₁, PM₂.₅, and PM₁₀ continuously at 5-minute intervals. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlations, t-tests, time-series decomposition, and occupational health risk assessment (ADD and HQ) following U.S. EPA methodology. Mean PM₂.₅ were 27.0 µg/m³ (Kotokoroba) and 28.9 µg/m³ (Kingsway), exceeding the WHO 24-hour guideline (15 µg/m³) on 61% and 92% of monitored days, and the Ghana EPA standard (25 µg/m³) on 44% and 78% of days. Mean PM₁₀ of 53.5 and 57.5 µg/m³ exceeded WHO limits on 50% and 43% of days. Seasonal peaks were observed during grain milling (June–August) at Kotokoroba (~ 30 µg/m³ PM₂.₅) and spice milling (December) at Kingsway (~ 35 µg/m³ PM₂.₅). Hazard Quotients exceeded 1.0 for PM₂.₅ (1.80 and 1.93) and PM₁₀ at both sites. Strong inter-fraction correlations ( r = 0.82–0.95, p-value ≤ 0.00) confirm shared milling emission sources. PM concentrations persistently exceed national and international guidelines, posing chronic occupational health risks. Wet processing, local exhaust ventilation, and staggered milling schedules are recommended. The study highlights the need for industry-specific PM standards. Limitations include absence of chemical composition analysis, no indoor–outdoor comparison, and no humidity correction for OPC readings.

items.title: Auditing Representation-Space Fraud Detection: A Bayesian IRL Framework for Calibrated Uncertainty and Its Limits
items.abstract: Shilling detectors for recommender systems are almost always evaluated by one number, detection AUROC, with no account of when it can be trusted. We audit representation-space detection with VEIL (Variational Evaluation via Inverse-reinforcement Learning), a pairwise (Bradley–Terry) Bayesian reward-inference framework over frozen encoder embeddings, after the Bayesian auditing paradigm for LLM alignment [1]: (A) a base posterior; (B) a hierarchical ARD extension with a learned confidence; and (C) a label-routed organic/attacker mixture used as an evidence-accumulation check. We prove (Prop. 1) that no detector built on a representation invariant to some transformation of user profiles can beat chance against an attack indistinguishable from organic profiles under that invariance. Detection is near-perfect against synthetic-structure attacks (AUROC 0.936–1.000) but collapses under donor-mimicry, which clones a real user’s item set and splices in 1–3 target items: to chance on MovieLens-1M (0.48–0.51), partially on Amazon Musical Instruments, and least on CiaoDVD. Donor-mimicry is not undetectable: a non-learned baseline, each profile’s maximum raw item-set Jaccard similarity to any other, reaches AUROC 0.92–0.97 (average precision 0.50–0.57) on all four donor-mimicry configurations, including ML-1M, where every embedding-based score is at chance. The signal is in the raw profiles; LightGCN’s representation discards it, placing injected profiles closer to their true donor than its zero-propagation MF reduction does (distance 1.98 vs. 3.09). Severity varies by dataset, encoder, and detection method, with no one axis predicting the others. The limit lies in the representation, not the attack, and raw-similarity checks are a necessary complement to any learned detector

items.title: AUGMANITAI: Tracing Self-Definition in Intensive Human–AI Practice
items.abstract: Working paper v1.0. Manuscript prepared on 18 November 2026; evidence review completed through 9 November 2026. Not externally peer reviewed. How does an intensive human–AI practice become an explicit account of the person practising it, and how might that account relate to later action? This paper reconstructs Andreas Ehstand's January 2026 formulation of AUGMANITAI through retained dialogue, correspondence, manuscripts and public records. The selected exchanges preserve human naming, questions about self-application, model-generated proposals, corrections and publication decisions. Correspondence anchors early activity in 2023 and subsequent work; archived pages document a named project-subject account by 29 January 2026. The evidence supports attribution of the particular formulation while preserving tensions between the public account and its framing. Independent dates anchor particular records, rather than validating all experiences described within them. Four later cases document publication, public interpretation, executable production and specifically credited reuse by another author. They show different forms of outward activity without isolating an effect of self-definition or AI assistance on capability. The contribution is a documentary reconstruction and a comparative framework separating three questions: how a self-description formed, whether subsequent practice changed, and what happened outside the dialogue. A reusable episode report specifies evidence, missing links and competing explanations. This approach supports comparison across differently named practices without presuming a new human classification or a demonstrated developmental mechanism. The PDF includes a comparative framework, an episode-reporting template and selected evidence in Appendix B. Raw correspondence and private dialogue archives are not released. AI systems assisted literature review, source analysis and drafting.

items.title: Automation, Growth, and Distribution: A Classical View
items.abstract: Fears that machines will displace workers have recurred for two centuries, and artificial intelligence has revived them. The leading macroeconomic models of automation assume perfect competition and full employment, so the wage clears the labor market and wage-setting institutions play no role. This article takes automation capital, machines that perform work otherwise done by people, from that literature and rebuilds the analysis on Classical-Marxian foundations, with a wage fixed by collective bargaining and labor abundant at that wage. Labor demand becomes a residual of the accumulation decision, and the share of profits directed toward automation rather than ordinary capital becomes a determinant of distribution. Below a critical value of that share, the economy grows along a balanced path with a constant labor share, which capitalists can lower by automating more. Above that value the labor share collapses to zero. Whether automation raises or lowers growth depends on the level of the institutionally set wage and on the planning horizon of capital. When a union sets the wage, the threat of automation alone moderates its demands, so no automation occurs in equilibrium while distribution is still shaped by it. Implications for taxation and democratic stability are discussed.

items.title: AWARENESS AND ATTITUDE OF LIBRARIANS TOWARD ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE FOR EFFECTIVE SERVICE DELIVERY IN UNIVERSITY LIBRARIES IN TARABA STATE, NIGERIA
items.abstract: University libraries are expected to provide fast, accurate, and technology-driven information services to support students, researchers, and academic staff. Although artificial intelligence (AI) tools can enhance cataloguing, reference services, and information retrieval, service delivery in many university libraries in Taraba State remains predominantly manual. Preliminary observations also indicate gaps in librarians’ awareness and attitudes toward AI, yet the extent to which these factors influence service delivery is unclear. This study examined librarians’ awareness and attitudes toward AI tools and their effect on information service delivery in university libraries in Taraba State. A descriptive survey design was adopted, involving 122 librarians from Federal University Wukari (FUW), Taraba State University (TSU) Jalingo, and Kwararafa University Wukari (KUW). Data from 117 valid questionnaires were analyzed using descriptive statistics and one-way ANOVA at the 0.05 significance level. Results showed a high level of AI awareness among librarians (overall mean = 4.19), with KUW exhibiting the highest consistency, followed by TSU and FUW. Attitudes toward AI were also strongly positive across all institutions (overall mean = 4.41). ANOVA revealed significant institutional differences in awareness (p = .000 < .05) and attitudes (p = .002 < .05), attributed to variations in training, exposure, and institutional support. The study concludes that librarians’ AI awareness and attitudes significantly shape the efficiency and quality of information service delivery. It recommends targeted AI training programmes, enhanced institutional support, and clear policy frameworks to strengthen AI adoption in university libraries in Taraba State.

items.title: Bankruptcy Prediction via Hybrid Resampling and Stacking Ensemble Techniques with Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI)-Driven Analysis
items.abstract: Abstract Reliable bankruptcy prediction is essential for creditors, investors, auditors, and regulators because delayed identification of financial distress can result in substantial economic losses. However, bankruptcy is a rare event, and severe class imbalance can produce high overall accuracy while concealing poor detection of distressed firms. This study develops an integrated bankruptcy prediction framework using the Taiwanese Bankruptcy Prediction dataset. Five boosting classifiers and five deep learning models were evaluated as standalone models. A two-stage stacking procedure subsequently used five-fold out-of-fold predictions from the boosting models as inputs to the deep learning meta-learners. The results show that resampling strategy materially shaped model behavior. SVM-SMOTE and SMOTE-Tomek favored accuracy and specificity, whereas SMOTE-ENN delivered stronger minority-class detection. Among standalone models, the RNN with SVM-SMOTE achieved the best overall predictive balance, with recall of 0.8235, G-mean of 0.8639, and ROC-AUC of 0.9417. Among stacking ensembles, SMOTE-ENN with (GB+XGB+HGB+LGBM+AB) + LSTM provided the best results with recall of 0.7255, G-mean of 0.8254, and ROC-AUC of 0.9270. SHAP analysis further showed that predicted bankruptcy risk was driven primarily by profitability, solvency and capital structure, debt-servicing burden, and operational efficiency and cost pressure. The findings demonstrate that no single resampling-model configuration universally dominates; therefore, model selection should reflect whether the operational priority is overall classification performance or the detection of bankrupt firms. The proposed framework provides an interpretable and leakage-controlled approach for aligning bankruptcy prediction with different financial risk-management objectives.

items.abstract: This repository provides the analytical dataset, feature dictionary, cohort summaries, model specifications, and executable Python analysis workflow supporting reproducible analysis of behavioral patterns and cognitive accountability failures in human-AI decision systems across controlled laboratory, flight simulation, and operational aviation settings. The repository contains the analytical data structure used for classification experiments, including 127 engineered behavioral features, outcome labels, cohort information, feature definitions, model specifications, and reproducibility documentation. The analysis workflow implements the reported machine-learning methodology, including data partitioning, class-imbalance handling, Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, Logistic Regression, ensemble prediction, stacking, early prediction, study-specific evaluation, grouped validation, and domain-shift evaluation. The repository is intended to provide a transparent computational record of the analytical workflow and facilitate independent examination of the reported methodology and model evaluation procedures. Operationally sensitive, confidential, or individually identifiable source records are not included.

Across a four-model panel and four objective-grafted checkpoints we find the three layers measurable but loosely coupled: self-rewriting chains preserve the verbal directive while the revealed maximand drifts — spontaneous avowal—operative decoupling, without any adversarial training. Weight grafts move allocation and avowal asymmetrically, and a human—judge of 0.22 shows the classification boundary itself is observer-relative. items.title: Beyond “She’ll be right”: Building the Habit of Health for the Next Generation of Workplace Health
items.abstract: What if the very people responsible for protecting workplace health and safety are unintentionally standing in the way of support? WorkSafe New Zealand's 2025 Workforce Insights Programme, surveying 1,643 employers and 1,824 workers, revealed a concerning disconnect. While 88% of employers believed health and safety risks were discussed openly and helpfully, only 64% of workers agreed. This 24-percentage-point perception gap raises an uncomfortable question for health and safety professionals: Are we opening pathways to support, or becoming the gatekeepers who prevent people from accessing it? With five generations in New Zealand's workforce and increasing cultural diversity, workers communicate concerns and seek support differently. Complex reporting processes, delayed responses and assumptions about what workers need can discourage early help-seeking, allowing injuries, burnout and psychosocial risks to escalate. Drawing on Habit Health's experience in occupational health, injury management, rehabilitation and Employee Assistance Programme (EAP) services, the presentation highlights the value of early intervention. Habit Health's rehabilitation programme reported reductions in average compensation days from 147 to 56, average claim costs from $23,500 to $14,100, and return-to-work time from 238 to 118 days, alongside patient satisfaction of 9.6/10. Drawing from the success of the program while challenging traditional approaches, I introduce the G.A.T.E. framework. Through this I am encouraging health and safety professionals to: G: Give permission to speak up. A: Ask and act early when warning signs emerge. T: Tailor pathways to individual needs. E: Evidence the response and demonstrate tangible improvements. Through timely clinical intervention, accessible counselling, workplace rehabilitation and proactive occupational health support, Habit Health demonstrates how organisations can turn early warning signs into meaningful action. Every health and safety professional influences the gate. The question is whether your actions are helping people walk through it.

items.title: Beyond access: the evolution of Portugal’s pharmacy-based vaccination strategy and the future role of AI-driven outreach
items.abstract: Vaccination programmes increasingly face a paradox: expanding access does not necessarily translate into coverage at policy targets. Portugal provides an instructive example. The integration of community pharmacies into seasonal influenza and COVID-19 vaccination created more than 3,500 vaccination points and approximately 70% of influenza doses were administered in pharmacies in 2023–2024. The pharmacy share then fell to under 46% by 2025–2026, while total influenza doses remained broadly stable (2.41 to 2.56 million per season). This indicates a redistribution of doses across settings rather than a loss of vaccination activity; changes in age eligibility, high-dose vaccination for adults aged ≥85 years in SNS units, and invitation and recall activity may all have contributed. Influenza coverage among adults aged ≥65 years remained below the World Health Organization target of 75%, at 70.5% in 2024–2025 and 73.0% in 2025–2026. This suggests that, residual under-vaccination reflects barriers beyond physical access. The authors use “activation gap” descriptively for potentially addressable interruptions between eligibility and vaccination. Portugal already uses registry-based invitations and reminders, the open question is what a conversational layer, scripted or based on generative AI, could add. Evidence is relatively strong for reminders, growing for scripted conversational interventions and preliminary for generative AI. The authors therefore propose a registry-based randomised comparison of existing recall, existing recall plus a scripted conversational intervention, and existing recall plus a generative-AI conversational intervention, with incremental vaccination, safety, equity, trust and cost per additional vaccinated person as outcomes.

items.abstract: The emergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and computational technologies has introduced newpossibilities for literary interpretation within Digital Humanities. This study explores the potential ofhuman–AI collaboration in extending the boundaries of traditional close reading and computational distantreading through Kazuo Ishiguro’s Klara and the Sun (2021). Drawing on Franco Moretti’s concept ofDistant Reading, the research investigates how computational methods and AI-assisted textual analysis canidentify recurring patterns, thematic structures, character relationships, and emotional representations withinthe novel. The study adopts a mixed-methods approach that integrates qualitative close reading withqualitative computational analysis. AI tools are employed to examine textual patterns and generateinterpretive insights, which are subsequently evaluated against human critical readings. The paper alsoexamines the interpretive limitations of AI, particularly in understanding contextual nuances, symbolism,ambiguity, and emotional complexity.

items.title: Beyond memorisation: reforming legal education in Nigeria for digital innovation, practical competence and sustainable development
items.abstract: Legal education in Nigeria operates through a two-stage structure comprising a five-year university programme and a subsequent one-year professional training at the Nigerian Law School. While the latter introduces practical skills through advocacy, drafting, simulations and clinical attachments, this paper argues that the principal pedagogical deficiencies originate in the university phase. Instruction at this level remains dominated by rote memorisation, passive lectures and examination-driven teaching, raising concerns about graduate readiness in a legal environment increasingly shaped by digitalisation and artificial intelligence. Using doctrinal and empirical methods, including curriculum analysis and structured questionnaires administered to lecturers and students across four universities in four Nigerian states, the study identifies a persistent gap between recognition of the need for reform and continued reliance on traditional instructional models. The findings reveal substantial challenges for both teachers and students in adapting to innovative pedagogies, including limited pedagogical training, institutional inertia, large class sizes, resource constraints and student uncertainty about non-memorisation-based assessment. Although professional legal training provides a more practice-oriented experience, its limited duration restricts its capacity to remedy foundational weaknesses. The paper argues for embedding skills-based, reflective, digitally informed and interdisciplinary pedagogies within the university curriculum, supported by sustained faculty capacity building.

items.title: Beyond Operational Fluency: A Three-Tier AI Literacy Architecture for Reskilling and Upskilling in Strategic Talent Development
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) occupies two positions in talent development simultaneously: the principal driver of the reskilling imperative, obsoleting skills faster than organizations can replace them, and increasingly the instrument through which reskilling is delivered, via adaptive platforms, generated content, and automated coaching. Reskilling scholarship assumes training technology is causally independent of the skill shift it responds to, an assumption prior industrial transitions permitted but AI's shared mechanism no longer does. This conceptual paper argues that AI's dual position generates five failure modes conventional reskilling models cannot detect: velocity without capability, a deskilling loop in which the instrument reproduces the condition it was deployed to remedy, personalization that fragments collective capability, stratified access that widens the divide reskilling was meant to close, and erosion of the entry-level roles through which experiential learning occurs. Drawing on integrative reviews of AI and workers' skills, Industry 4.0 reskilling blueprints, and AI governance scholarship, the paper applies the HUMAN framework (Human Oversight, Upskilling for AI Literacy, Meaningful Augmentation, Accountability and Audit, Networked Learning) to each failure mode, and extends its upskilling principle into a three-tier AI literacy architecture, operational fluency, evaluative literacy, and complementary capability, that depreciates at rates inverse to the investment it typically attracts. The paper translates this into five testable propositions and offers implementation guidance differentiated by organizational context.

items.title: BEYOND PERSONALIZATION: METACOGNITIVE AI SCAFFOLDING FOR MULTILINGUAL LEARNERS OF ENGLISH IN INDIA
items.abstract: Integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI) into English language education has created new opportunitiesfor personalised, adaptive, and learner-centred instruction. However, multilingual learners in Indiaencounter distinctive challenges arising from linguistic diversity, unequal language proficiency,mother-tongue interference, and differences in educational backgrounds. Although conventional AIpowered personalisation provides individualised content and feedback, it often prioritises immediateperformance improvement rather than developing learners’ awareness of their own learning processes.To address this limitation, the present study proposes Metacognitive AI Scaffolding as an innovativepedagogical approach that moves beyond personalisation toward conscious, reflective, and selfregulated English language learning. The study examines how AI-based scaffolding can supportmultilingual learners in planning, monitoring, evaluating, and regulating their language-learningstrategies. Using a qualitative, conceptual research methodology, the study draws on existing literatureon artificial intelligence in education, metacognition, scaffolding, multilingual pedagogy, and selfregulated learning. It explores the potential of AI tools to provide reflective prompts, diagnosticfeedback, guided questioning, and adaptive learning support while recognising learners’ multilingualbackgrounds. The proposed framework seeks to reposition AI from a content-delivery mechanism toa metacognitive learning partner. Ultimately, the study contributes to an inclusive and learner-centredframework for English language education in India by strengthening learner autonomy, criticalreflection, and multilingual competence.

items.title: Beyond security: why AI-mediated prison visitation must be fair, transparent, and human-centered
items.abstract: Prison visitation is usually administered as a security operation, yet it is also a relational and rehabilitative intervention. Rule 58 of the Nelson Mandela Rules provides for regular contact with family and friends through correspondence, telecommunications and visits (United Nations, 2015). A meta-analysis of 16 studies associated visitation with a 26% reduction in recidivism, although effects varied by visit type, outcome, gender and follow-up (Mitchell et al., 2016). This is not a universal causal guarantee, but it shows that access to visitation is not a minor administrative convenience.Digital visitation can widen access for families separated by distance, cost, illness or disability. Video visits can help incarcerated fathers take part in children's daily lives, while raising problems of timing, technology and the absence of touch (Duursma et al., 2024;Hanley et al., 2024), and users may value remote access while still preferring in-person contact (Murdoch and King, 2020). Remote systems can also reduce agency, comprehension and privacy for people already disadvantaged (McKay and Macintosh, 2024). The appropriate policy is complementarity, not substitution. Video conferencing alone is not artificial intelligence (AI). We use AI-mediated visitation to mean pathways in which AI informs identity verification, scheduling, translation, risk flagging, content moderation, interruption or post-visit review. The 2026 UNODC-ICRC Handbook states that video visits should supplement in-person visits and that AI in prisons should be fair, explainable, contestable and under human control (UNODC and ICRC, 2026). We argue that these principles require a specific rule: AI may assist access and safety, but it should never be the sole basis for denying, suspending or terminating family contact.Transparency, accountability, auditing and human oversight are established principles (Kroll et al., 2017;Ananny and Crawford, 2018;UNESCO, 2021;OECD, 2024;Cheong, 2024), and the Council of Europe has already adapted them to prisons and probation (Council of Europe, 2024). We do not claim to originate them. Our contribution is to show where general frameworks stop short when the decision concerns family contact, and to supply three elements they lack.First, a consequence-tiered classification (Table 1) separates assistive functions from gatekeeping, interventional and inferential ones, so that safeguards scale with consequence rather than applying uniformly to "prison AI". Second, a relational-irreversibility criterion: a missed visit, a child's birthday call or a terminated conversation cannot be restored by a later appeal, so review must occur before or during the contact window. General frameworks treat remedy as retrospective; visitation requires prospective or same-session remedy. Third, third-party standing: visitors are not detainees, yet their faces, voices and devices are processed. Frameworks oriented to the detained person rarely give families an independent right to notice, correction and appeal. Rapid gains in AI capability do not settle these questions, because reliability, interpretability and evaluation remain open problems even in well-resourced scientific domains (Xu et al., 2026); they are harder still in a coercive setting with contested ground truth.We distinguish documented evidence from hypothetical scenarios; Supplementary Table S1 lists each source and its evidential status.A national survey of US video-visitation contracts found that 74% of jails adopting video visitation eliminated in-person visits, and some vendor contracts required this (Rabuy and Wagner, 2015). In England, a 2018-2019 trial scanned the faces of 770 visitors at HMP Humber; some visitors turned back on learning of the scans, and campaigners warned that deterring families would be counter-productive (Prison Legal News, 2019). During the COVID-19 pandemic, prisons in England and Wales introduced video calls using software with facial recognition (Ministry of Justice, 2020); family guidance at one prison warned that background photographs could disrupt recognition and end calls prematurely (HMP Forest Bank, 2020), and the supplier advertised emotion recognition to detect changes in mood (Made Purple Ltd, n.d.). In the United States, AI transcription and keyword alerting of prisoners' calls has been adopted by state and federal agencies, while families and advocates have raised concerns about misinterpretation and racial bias (Route Fifty, 2021;Correctional News, 2026). Outside prisons, Australia's Robodebt inquiry showed how automated decisions without adequate human review can cause serious and widespread harm (Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme, 2023).A visitor whose face fails verification on a poor-quality phone camera is refused a call with no manual alternative; an emotion-inference flag labels a crying child's conversation "agitated" and prompts termination. We present these as scenarios that the documented features above make plausible, not as reported incidents.The framework does not pretend these values align. Security versus rights: contraband and witness intimidation are real, but a system optimised only for detected incidents is misspecified, because its costs, such as false rejections, deterred visits and abandoned contact, fall on families, who already face burdensome visiting procedures (Boppre et al., 2022), and are rarely measured. Efficiency versus oversight: automation saves staff time precisely by reducing human scrutiny, and reviewers tend to defer to automated alerts (Parasuraman and Manzey, 2010); nominal oversight can then legitimise unreliable outputs (Green, 2022). Transparency versus gaming: full disclosure of detection rules may help circumvention, yet a bare reference to "security reasons" prevents correction and undermines legitimacy (Tyler, 2006). We resolve this by requiring an individual, actionable reason and disclosure of decision rules to an independent auditor even where public disclosure is limited. Public duty versus commercial incentive: where vendors are paid per call or per minute, contract terms can shape visitation policy (Rabuy and Wagner, 2015), so procurement is itself a governance instrument.Table 1 specifies, for each tier, minimum safeguards, appeal routes, review timelines, audit duties and measurable fairness indicators. Three features carry the argument. Appeals are two-stage: an on-site supervisor with authority to override decisions within the same session, followed by written review within 72 hours or before the next scheduled visit, whichever is sooner, with escalation to a body independent of the prison. Accountability is named: each consequential deployment has a responsible official, tamperevident decision logs, and contracts that prohibit in-person bans and guarantee auditor access to data. Fairness is measured through disaggregated false-rejection rates, override rates and appeal outcomes, with predefined disparity thresholds that trigger suspension pending review. This treats trustworthiness as a lifecycle responsibility rather than a launch certificate (Tabassi, 2023). The numerical values in Table 1 are proposed starting points for calibration, not validated standards.Three red lines follow the irreversibility criterion. No adverse visitation decision may rest solely on AI output; biometric failure must trigger an alternative verification route rather than exclusion; and speech, behaviour or emotion inference must never be treated as established misconduct. Where immediate intervention is necessary for safety, it should be temporary, documented, proportionate and promptly reviewed.These requirements will land differently. In the European Union, the AI Act classifies emotion recognition and many biometric and law-enforcement uses as high-risk and gives affected persons a right to an explanation, yet its prohibition of emotion recognition covers workplaces and education, not detention (European Union, 2024). Malaysia has no AI-specific statute; its national AI governance guidelines are voluntary (MOSTI, 2024), and its Personal Data Protection Act 2010 does not apply to federal and state governments (Malaysia, 2010). Its prison service already combines online booking with in-person and video visits (Berita Harian, 2024), so AI could be added without a dedicated legal framework. In the United States, visitation technology is often procured county by county (Rabuy and Wagner, 2015), and familyengagement policies differ markedly between states (Pappas et al., 2024).Resources also differ. We therefore propose a minimum floor applicable everywhere, consisting of the red lines, a non-digital route, same-session human override and incident logging, and an enhanced tier of independent audits, disaggregated reporting and impact assessment for systems with adequate capacity. Where independent review bodies are absent, an existing ombudsman, inspectorate or human-rights commission can be designated. Low capacity justifies restricting AI to assistive functions; it does not justify weaker safeguards for gatekeeping ones.The framework is normative and should be tested. We propose five questions.• RQ1. Do false-rejection rates of biometric visitor verification differ by age, skin tone, disability and device quality, and does a manual fallback close the resulting gap in completed visits? Laboratory testing already shows demographic differentials across face-recognition algorithms (Grother et al., 2019). Design: disaggregated audit of operational logs.• RQ2. Does introducing an AI-assisted pathway change completed visits, cancellations and inperson visit numbers? Design: stepped-wedge rollout across facilities. • RQ3. How often do reviewers override automated flags, and does this change with time pressure and access to underlying evidence? Design: log analysis of staff interviews. • RQ4. Which explanation formats enable families to identify and correct errors? Design:randomised vignette experiments with visitors. • RQ5. Does same-session review reduce irreversible relational harm compared with retrospective appeal? Design: comparison of family-reported visit quality and appeal outcomes across sites.Evaluation should combine security indicators with relational and procedural outcomes, report who is excluded, and involve incarcerated people and families in defining success.AI is not inherently incompatible with humane visitation. It may reduce delays, improve translation and extend contact when travel is impossible. The test is institutional purpose and the affected person's practical capacity to understand, challenge and correct an outcome before relational harm becomes irreversible. Preserve in-person visitation; use video to expand contact; tier AI functions by consequence; prohibit solely automated adverse decisions; and measure success by whether families keep safe, dignified and meaningful contact.

items.title: Beyond stickie notes: if it’s not tracked did it happen?
items.abstract: Human Factors (HF) practitioners can be drawn to the more visible aspects of the discipline: end user engagement, task analysis, usability assessment, design innovation etc. Lesser attention is given to the less glamorous, and often less celebrated, work that occurs after the data collection is concluded and the analyse is complete. Yet for many HF practitioners, a significant proportion of HF effort can be dedicated to reporting, assurance, issue management, compliance demonstration, audit responses, and evidence gathering. These activities are sometimes perceived as administrative overheads rather than core HF practice. This presentation challenges that perception.

items.title: Beyond the tool: a systematic realist synthesis of cognitive agency in human-GenAI interaction in higher education
items.abstract: Abstract Cognitive agency concerns learners’ effortful, self-directed control over reasoning with generative AI (GenAI). Building on an existing implementation-level classification of generative AI use, this review examines how cognitive work is allocated between learners and AI tools. Following PRISMA 2020, searches of Scopus and Web of Science (2021–2025) yielded 93 peer-reviewed studies, appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. A realist synthesis specified an a priori program theory crossing the type of work offloaded (extraneous versus germane; cognitive load theory) with processing of AI output (heuristic acceptance versus analytical scrutiny; dual-process theory), and audited the evidence on each axis under manifest coding (reported evidence only) and latent coding (adding design-based inference). Under manifest coding, 21 studies were located on both axes; all four configurations occurred, two in a single study each, and the nine Cognitive Extension studies reported peripheral uses with analytical scrutiny. Of the 93 studies, 49 reported no learner behavior toward AI output, 69 reported no learning measure independent of AI assistance, and four reported processing evidence together with such a measure. Group differences or part-sample outcomes were documented in 30 studies; one further study reported stage differences, but no learner-, task-, or assessment-level moderator showed an interpretable corpus-level association with substitution. This evidence profile identifies the process and AI-independent learning measures needed to distinguish cognitive extension from cognitive substitution. The review restates the Heterogeneous Pathways of Distributed Agency (HPDA) Model as seven testable propositions and specifies the process-tracing and AI-independent outcome designs needed to test them.

items.title: Beyond the tool: what a course-aligned AI assistant reveals about student learning in microbiology
items.abstract: Course-aligned artificial intelligence (AI) tutors are increasingly offered as learning support in higher education. Beyond providing practice and feedback, they may also help teachers identify gaps in understanding across a cohort. In a second-year medical microbiology and immunology unit of 500 to 800 students, a course-aligned AI assistant built on The University of Sydney’s Cogniti platform gave students scenario-based short-answer practice with rubric-referenced feedback. Its conversation logs turned out to be a diagnostic instrument. Across more than 1300 conversations, the logs revealed cohort-level knowledge gaps and recurring terminology errors mid-semester. An exploratory analysis also found small positive correlations between practice-oriented use of the assistant and final short-answer marks, although these findings should be interpreted cautiously. The gaps were fed back to the class through an interactive revision resource used in lectures. These insights could be obtained through three approaches requiring different levels of technical expertise: the platform’s own no-code summaries, method-led coding with basic programming, and specialist computational analysis. We also discuss how the approach can be adapted where no equivalent platform exists. The project highlights that a course-aligned AI assistant can provide valuable insight into cohort-level understanding of the subject.

items.title: Blending seamless and seamful tactics to nurture practical and reflexive AI competences in design education
items.abstract: The rapid integration of generative AI into design education generates tensions between innovation and pedagogy. This paper presents a pilot program that combines structured spaces for practical learning and critical reflection on generative AI. Implemented within a large undergraduate Storytelling and Animation course, the program combined seamless AI-based creative exercises with a deliberately seamful activity intended to disrupt automation and foreground human agency. By analysing student reflections collected through written reports, we find that this pedagogical program can foster diverse critical positionings, enabling students to negotiate authorship, question tool dependencies, and reappropriate creative processes. Rather than adopting or rejecting generative AI uncritically, students developed nuanced understandings of its role in their design practices. The main contribution of this work is to foreground the combination of seamless and seamful activities as a pedagogical tactic for teaching practical competences while encouraging critical reflexivity about the integration of generative AI into higher education.

items.title: Body appreciation and sport participation motivation in female athletes: the mediating role of objectified body consciousness and the moderating role of sport type (aesthetic versus non-aesthetic)
items.abstract: Introduction Female athletes train in settings where the body serves at once as an instrument of performance and as an object of evaluation. Whether body appreciation relates to the quality of sport participation motivation, and through which psychological route, remains underexamined. Drawing on objectification theory and self-determination theory, this study tested whether objectified body consciousness, operationalized as body surveillance and body shame, statistically accounts for that association, and whether the first stage of the indirect route differs between aesthetic and non-aesthetic sports. Methods Chinese female university athletes ( N = 452; 201 aesthetic, 251 non-aesthetic) from six universities in Henan and Xinjiang completed the Body Appreciation Scale-2, the Objectified Body Consciousness Scale, and the intrinsic motivation subscale of the Sport Motivation Scale-II. Confirmatory factor analysis and tests of configural, metric, and scalar measurement invariance preceded the estimation of a first-stage moderated mediation model (PROCESS Model 7) with 5,000 bias-corrected bootstrap resamples. Results The four-factor measurement model fit acceptably, χ 2 (371) = 651.54, χ 2 /df = 1.76, CFI = 0.960, TLI = 0.956, RMSEA = 0.041, SRMR = 0.049, and invariance held across sport type (all |ΔCFI| < = 0.004). Higher body appreciation went together with higher intrinsic motivation (total B = 0.650, p < 0.001), and objectified body consciousness carried part of that association. Its negative link with body appreciation was stronger in aesthetic sports (interaction B = −0.358, p < 0.001, Δ R 2 = 0.024), giving conditional indirect associations of 0.284 [95% CI (0.200, 0.385)] and 0.100 [95% CI (0.036, 0.166)]; the index of moderated mediation was 0.185 [95% CI (0.089, 0.295)]. Two alternative orderings of the same variables fitted worse or reversed the sign pattern. Discussion Body appreciation is a relevant correlate of motivational quality in women’s sport, and the appearance-saturated climate of aesthetic disciplines merits particular applied attention. This design is cross-sectional and each category aggregates heterogeneous disciplines, so these implications remain provisional pending longitudinal and experimental verification.

items.title: Breast Ultrasound Classification Under Cross-Dataset Shift: A Multi-Seed Benchmark of Convolutional Networks, a Vision Transformer, and a Self-Supervised Foundation Model
items.abstract: Deep-learning classifiers for breast ultrasound are usually evaluated on images from their training institution, and self-supervised foundation models are increasingly proposed as more transferable than supervised networks; whether ranking ability, decision thresholds, and probability calibration survive a change in institution has rarely been tested under leakage-controlled conditions. We fine-tuned ResNet-50, EfficientNet-B0, a supervised Vision Transformer (ViT-B/16), and self-supervised DINOv2 under one shared protocol on the official BUS-BRA five-fold partitions, each fold with three seeds, and on three case-grouped hold-out splits, and evaluated every trained model unchanged on the Breast Ultrasound Images (BUSI) dataset. The supervised models largely retained their discrimination externally. ResNet-50 had the highest mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve under the official folds, but no criterion separated it from ViT-B/16, whose small hold-out advantage at the decision threshold did not recur. In every official-fold run, both models labeled a larger share of BUSI than of BUS-BRA images malignant, although prevalence was the same—a shift that temperature scaling cannot correct. Top-label calibration error also understated malignant-class miscalibration. Full-frame DINOv2 did not fit its training data in any run, although exploratory lesion cropping produced good discrimination. External evaluations should report operating-point transport and class-wise calibration alongside discrimination.

items.title: Bringing Specificity to Workplace Affordances: Operationalising Learning at Work
items.abstract: Abstract In workplace learning (WPL) research, workplace affordances concern possibilities for participation and learning that arise in relation to people, work practices and their social and material arrangements. These possibilities vary across professional groups and circumstances, while learning also depends on how individuals engage in work. This article proposes a tentative framework for analysing that variation by bringing Billett’s (2001) account of co-participation into dialogue with Davis and Chouinard’s (2017) theorisation of affordances. It adapts six mechanisms – request, demand, allow, encourage, discourage and refuse – to examine how possibilities for participation are shaped in workplace practice. It also considers how perception, dexterity and legitimacy shape what is possible for different professionals and whether and how they engage. Examples from the implementation of e-health tools in Swedish primary care illustrate how a workplace change can open up participation for some professional groups while constraining it for others. The framework offers a way to analyse for whom opportunities arise, how they are encountered and under what circumstances they are taken up. It may inform future WPL research and analyses of technology implementation in practice.

items.title: Calibrated reliance on generative-AI health advice: a perspective on correctness, risk, and escalation
items.abstract: Members of the public increasingly consult generative artificial intelligence (AI) for health advice, and research has largely asked whether they trust it. Trust is the wrong yardstick. Reliance on health advice is appropriate only when it tracks whether the advice is correct and what an error would cost. We argue for an outcome standard, calibrated reliance, under which four actions (adopt, verify, reject, and escalate to professional care) are judged jointly against advice correctness and the cost of error. Drawing on trust calibration, automation bias, algorithm aversion, advice taking, and heuristic models of credibility, we read a purposive set of human-participant studies against this standard. The studies show both reliance errors. Identical advice is discounted when labeled as AI-generated, which is consistent with underreliance. Low-accuracy AI responses are rated and followed much like physicians' responses, and lay users assisted by large language models choose care dispositions no better than controls, which is consistent with overreliance. Both patterns suggest that lay reliance responds to source and fluency cues more than to correctness. Interventions that require users to act, such as verification affordances, cognitive forcing, and expressed uncertainty, show more promise than passive labels, but no study has yet manipulated correctness and graded clinical risk together while observing verification and escalation. We state five propositions with their evidential status, operational definitions, and a factorial design that would test them.

items.title: Campaigns That Click: Unleashing the Power of Push Notifications on Mobile Apps
items.abstract: Push notifications can do more than promote a single merchant: They can redirect attention across an entire mobile marketplace. Drawing on more than 200 campaigns, 60 million user-campaign observations, and two controlled experiments, this study shows that notifications substantially increase same-day engagement with advertised merchants while also generating meaningful spillovers to other merchants within and across categories. Effectiveness varies by merchant, user, message design, and delivery timing. Notifications tend to work especially well for less prominent merchants, newer users, Android users, deeper discounts, urgency cues, and carefully timed delivery. However, repeated exposure produces diminishing returns and can eventually reduce engagement as annoyance and attentional overload increase. For platform managers, the findings support managing notifications as a portfolio rather than evaluating campaigns in isolation: targeting, message design, timing, cross-merchant benefits, and cumulative frequency should be optimized jointly. Platforms should also incorporate spillover value into campaign pricing, performance reporting, and merchant communication. For policymakers and platform-governance leaders, the results underscore the importance of meaningful consent, frequency controls, and transparent notification practices that protect user attention while preserving the economic benefits of timely, relevant mobile communication.
