items.title: Carbon-aware scheduling of large language model training across multiple US power grid operators: a marginal emissions analysis
items.abstract: Abstract The rapid expansion of data center infrastructure, accelerated by the growing computational demands of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), has led to an unprecedented increase in electricity consumption. As AI developers race to deploy GenAI products, time-to-market pressure drives continuous model training that demands baseload power, often from high-CO 2 emissions sources like natural gas and coal instead of intermittent renewables like wind and solar. Carbon-aware strategies that shift model training in real time to periods or locations with cleaner power on the margin have emerged as a near-term decarbonization lever, but the relative effectiveness of temporal flexibility (pausing model training during high-carbon hours) versus spatial flexibility (migrating workloads to cleaner grid regions) remains poorly understood under real-world constraints. This study evaluates these strategies using 2025 marginal operating CO 2 emissions rate (MOER) data from WattTime across 43 subregions spanning four US grid operators: California Independent System Operator (CAISO), Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), Midcontinent Independent System Operator, and Pennsylvania–Jersey–Maryland (PJM). Using Meta’s LLaMA 3.1 model family as representative workloads, we simulate four scenarios: business-as-usual, reflecting a carbon-informed siting choice with no real-time operational flexibility (S1, BAU); temporal flexibility with varying pause thresholds (S2); ideal spatial flexibility (S3); and spatial flexibility incorporating migration overhead (S4). We find that effective strategies are grid-dependent. In grids with high subregional MOER heterogeneity, spatial flexibility dominates: ERCOT achieves up to 36% emissions reduction via intraday alternation between wind-rich and solar-heavy zones, and the inter-ISO configuration achieves 67.3% reduction, with CAISO and ERCOT absorbing over 80% of training hours. In PJM, where subregional MOER profiles are largely homogeneous, spatial flexibility achieves only 0.3% emissions reduction while temporal flexibility reduces emissions by up to 17.2% relative to S1. The emissions-training time tradeoff under temporal flexibility is nonlinear: moderate reductions require marginal increases in training time, but near-zero emissions require nearly four times the baseline training duration. These findings provide grid-specific guidance for developers pursuing near-term decarbonization, and highlight opportunities for further improvement through empirical characterization of data migration overhead.

items.title: Cerebellar and Cerebellum-Like Computations for Novelty: Progress and Conceptual Models for Future Directions
items.abstract: Detecting novelty remains a persistent weakness of modern artificial intelligence (AI): systems that achieve impressive in-distribution accuracy can still fail under distribution shift, open-set conditions, and embodied settings where self-generated sensory changes confound external events. Nervous systems face closely related problems under tight constraints of latency, memory, and continual adaptation, suggesting that brain-inspired mechanisms may offer useful design principles rather than metaphors. This article reviews progress on two computational scenarios linking cerebellum and cerebellum-like circuits to novelty-related functions. The first, prediction–cancellation, learns sensory expectations from motor commands, state, context, and multimodal feedback, and subtracts predictable components via negative images, adaptive filtering, or internal forward models so that unpredicted external inputs emerge as residual signals. The second, high-dimensional expansion, transforms inputs into sparse, high-dimensional codes that alter similarity structure, reduce interference, and increase capacity; novelty and familiarity—along with set membership and frequency—can then be computed by plastic readouts. Although both scenarios can yield novelty-related signals, they define “novelty” differently and depend on different learning targets. Studies of the cerebellum proper most directly support prediction and residual coding of unexpected self-motion, whereas explicit memory-based novelty and familiarity readouts have been demonstrated most clearly in the Drosophila mushroom body. Finally, we connect these circuit-level ideas to recent AI algorithms and propose an explicitly conceptual model that integrates expansion coding with multi-timescale plasticity to support fast detection, short-term adaptation, and longer-term incorporation of persistent changes.

items.title: Changes in apparent system performance after post hoc human review of a large language model-generated benchmark for hospital wayfinding search: a comparative methodological evaluation
items.abstract: Background We developed a hospital web application that searches 266 destinations and links results to indoor navigation. Its default retrieval tiers run locally; an optional cloud large language model (LLM) tier requires explicit invocation. Synthetic queries were used because default-tier searches are not server-logged. Objective We examined how post hoc review of an LLM-generated benchmark changed the apparent benefit of completed system updates. Methods Version v2 added pronunciation aliases to v1; v3 added colloquial knowledge, pronunciation forms, destination-level score combination, and false-match rules. Two v3 rules were informed by evaluation-query failures. A clinician and a medical administrative coauthor jointly reviewed 563 synthetic queries without blinding, excluding 129 and rewriting 289 under review-defined policies. The final data contained 401 answerable and 33 no-valid-destination queries. Archived versions were compared across sequential review stages and with lexical and embedding implementations. Results Among the same 192 answerable evaluation-query identifiers and final accepted destinations, rewriting increased top-1 accuracy from 43.8% to 62.0% for v1 and from 56.8% to 63.0% for v3. Their difference remained near 13 percentage points through earlier review stages and decreased to 1.0 point at rewriting. The tested multilingual-E5-small implementation achieved higher top-3 accuracy than v3 (87.0% vs. 69.3%; exploratory P < 0.001), with differences in passage scoring, abstention, and evidence display. For v3, candidate returns occurred on 4/11 reviewed no-valid-destination evaluation queries and 11/29 original queries in a retrospective sensitivity analysis. Conclusions Unblinded benchmark editing changed performance estimates for frozen systems within this synthetic corpus. The findings do not establish improved real-user performance, independent generalization, or comparative clinical safety. The version difference is conditional on the review intervention; neither wording distribution was validated against patient input. Review before optimization and independent user evaluation require prospective assessment.

items.title: ChatGPT as an Instructor’s Assistant for Generating Chemistry Images: A Study Using ChatGPT Images 2.0
items.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence tools such as ChatGPT are increasingly being explored as assistants for chemistry instructors, including the preparation of teaching materials. Here, we examined whether ChatGPT, using Images 2.0, can generate scientifically correct images for first-year undergraduate chemistry students, focusing on visual and symbolic representations central to the discipline. A total of 444 images covering six chemistry areas were generated. Short, minimally descriptive prompts were used first; when important errors appeared, more detailed corrective prompts were introduced. We also generated instructional infographics combining several representations to explain chemical concepts. Scientific accuracy depended strongly on image complexity, with simpler orbitals, titration curves, and molecular structures generally performing better than more demanding examples. When the six categories were equally weighted, 43.5% of basic-prompt images, 45.6% of images from corrective prompts, and only 8.3% of instructional infographics were directly usable. Embedded text was generally more accurate than the images. Expert checking therefore remains essential before classroom use.

items.title: City-Level Sovereign Artificial Intelligence as a Valid Global Digital Compact Target: Topology, the Digital Agora and a Verifiable Cryptographic Stack for Localising the Compact
items.abstract: The Global Digital Compact, adopted by Member States in September 2024 as an annex to the Pact for the Future, sets shared objectives on digital divides, the digital economy, human rights online, data governance and the international governance of artificial intelligence. Whether those commitments matter depends on what happens in cities, where public services, infrastructure and community life meet digital systems. This paper argues that a city-level deployment of sovereign artificial intelligence is a valid and auditable target for the Compact's localisation, provided that democratic agency is written into the protocols that govern the system rather than left outside them. It brings together four bodies of work developed across a single line of inquiry. First, the topology of city-level AI: governance under Permanent Systemic Instability shifts from territorial monopoly to Flow Sovereignty, the maintenance of coherent, low-surprise trajectories across digital, physical and financial systems, organised through active inference, information-geometric policy navigation, sheaf-theoretic consensus and a 72-hour autonomy standard. Second, the Digital Agora, the rights-based counter-model to the Algorithmic Leviathan, which relocates democratic constraints from the political layer to the protocol layer. Third, the primitives that make such constraints enforceable: layered Sybil resistance, quadratic weighting of preference intensity, and the Minimal Anti-Collusion Infrastructure (MACI), which makes votes private, receipt-free and publicly tallied. Fourth, the cryptographic foundations of verification: zk-SNARKs, the per-circuit trusted setup of Groth16, the universal and updatable setup of PLONK, and Kate–Zaverucha–Goldberg polynomial commitments. The paper composes these into a six-layer deployment architecture, maps it to the Compact's five objectives, states five validity criteria a city deployment must meet, and sets out a pilot programme whose outputs are the local evidence the Compact asks for. It also states the limits: residual trust in setups and coordinators, the trade-off between Sybil resistance and inclusion, prover cost at city scale, and the sovereignty trap of new external dependencies. The work is a design specification; its single computation is an analytic illustration and contains no empirical data. KSCCN article prepared in connection with the GDC Localization Townhall, "Localizing the Global Digital Compact: From global frameworks to local implementation" (UN Office for Digital and Emerging Technologies, 18 November 2026). Companion to "City-Level AI: The Topology of Command and Information Geometry (Volume II)" (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22990597) and "The Algorithmic Leviathan" (Volume I, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.22990607). items.title: CLOF: A Coupled Framework for Quantifying Research Impacts via A Double Iterative Power Method
items.abstract: Research impact quantification plays a crucial role in academic assessment. Conventional citation-based metrics have several limitations in fair and comprehensive research evaluation. They often fail to recognize foundational work that receives limited early attention. They may also overlook sustained influence over time, differences across research fields, citation quality reflected by citation contexts and the expertise of citing authors, and variations in author contributions. We incorporate these aspects at the paper level through four factors: originality-oriented downstream influence, long-term influence, field-specific ranking, and citation quality. At the researcher level, we quantify credit according to author order. Based on these, we propose CLOF, a unified metric framework that quantifies the impacts of papers and researchers in an interdependent and iterative manner. To reduce reliance on manually specified weighting schemes, we employ multiple large language model (LLM)-based paper scorers. Their outputs are aggregated using an α-trimmed procedure to generate robust global signals for learning the combination weights. These learned weights further guide the coupled iterative updates of paper and researcher scores via a Double Iterative Power (DIP) method with theoretical convergence guarantees. Extensive experiments on academic datasets show that CLOF uncovers influence patterns across papers and researchers that are not captured by existing impact metrics.

items.title: CNN-ViT-Based Model Incorporating a Voting-Based Ensemble Method with Future Fusion for Multiple Sclerosis Classification
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is a chronic neurodegenerative disease affecting the central nervous system and significantly reducing the quality of life. Early detection of the disease is critical for slowing its progression and developing appropriate treatment plans. In recent years, artificial intelligence and deep learning methods have begun to play a significant role in clinical decision support systems, particularly due to their high accuracy rates in the analysis of Magnetic Resonance (MR) images. Methods: In this study, a hybrid model was developed for the automatic classification of MS. Two different architectures were used for feature extraction in the developed model. These architectures were selected from among the most successful architectures out of 10 different Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and Vision Transformer (ViT) architectures. Six different classifiers were used to classify the feature maps obtained in the proposed model and pre-trained models. The application of the VOTE operation in the final stage of the proposed model improved its performance. Results: The proposed model yielded competitive results compared to similar studies in the literature and the CNN and ViT architectures used in this study. The accuracy rate achieved with the proposed hybrid model was 97.28%. Conclusions: These results indicate that the proposed model has the potential to support computer-aided MS detection and may provide a useful framework for clinical decision support systems.

items.title: Cognitive Biases in Syllogistic Reasoning: A Comparative Study of Humans and Large Language Models
items.abstract: Understanding human cognitive processes for reasoning is a key step towards developing human-level AI reasoning systems. Syllogistic reasoning — a classical form of deductive reasoning — is a well-established paradigm for investigating human reasoning, known to elicit systematic cognitive biases such as belief bias and atmosphere effects. In this study, we compare the reasoning patterns of humans and three state-of-the-art Large Language Models (LLMs), namely GPT-4, GPT-4o and o4-mini, across multiple syllogism types with belief andatmosphere effects. Using an online questionnaire, we examine the biases in human syllogistic reasoning and compare this with the LLMs responses. We identify biases and differences in accuracy between different LLMs and humans. Belief-inconsistent statements, which contradict generally accepted common knowledge, and the atmosphere effect impact human and LLM answers. Our results show that, although LLMs outperform human participants, they exhibit human-like cognitive effects. We further evaluate the new reasoning model o4-mini, which performs nearly perfectly on the syllogism reasoning tasks and compare logic, human reasoning and LLM reasoning.

items.title: Cognitive effects of first- and third-person perspectives on navigational safety and efficiency in ship operation learning
items.abstract: Remote ship operation involves analysing information from various perspectives. However, a standardized educational approach for training remote ship operators is lacking. This study addresses the challenges posed by the cognitive attributes of individuals using remote ship operation and monitoring systems by investigating how different perspectives (first-vs. third-person) impact skill acquisition in ship operation. It introduces the ‘cognitive approach limit circle’ (CLC) concept, a decision-making criterion in ship operation, and formulate two hypotheses. The study conducted repeated ship operation trials from both perspectives in congested traffic scenarios over 100 iterations, analysing the learning trajectory regarding safety and efficiency. Accordingly, mitigating safety and efficiency inclination differences between perspectives is challenging. However, repeated exposure to ship operation experiences facilitates the acquisition of safety and efficiency skills that align with the cognitive attributes of the information utilized. Therefore, in training remote ship operators, initial emphasis on collision avoidance through exercises based on qualitative perceptual data—such as object orientation changes and distance perceived directly through retinal image alterations—rather than quantitative computer-generated information promotes the development of CLC awareness tailored to individual capabilities.

items.title: Collective Future Thinking About Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: How people imagine the future of artificial intelligence (AI) can play a significant role in shaping the development and use of AI. This study investigates collective future thinking about AI in emerging adults and factors that may influence the valence of the imagined events. Participants (N = 158) were asked to imagine, within 1 minute, as many worrying or exciting events about AI as they could that might happen in the near or distant futures. They also completed measures for their attitudes toward AI, technological readiness, and political ideology. Results showed that participants generated more worrying than exciting events for both near and distant futures. The worrying events primarily concerned ethical issues, unemployment, negative cognitive consequences of reliance on AI, and threats to humankind. Exciting events primarily involved scientific breakthroughs, increased efficiency, and assistance with learning, cognition, and well-being. Moreover, the more positive participants felt about AI and general technology, the more exciting relative to worrying events they imagined. Also, participants who self-identified as more conservative imagined more exciting relative to worrying events than those who self-identified as more liberal, and women imagined more worrying events than men. These original findings provide insights into the anticipatory process regarding AI and have societal implications for AI development and use.

items.title: Comparative analysis of LLM-based conversational agents as an assistive technology for web interaction
items.abstract: Abstract This study investigates whether LLM-based Conversational Agents (LLMCAs) could be employed as assistive technologies, helping anyone navigate a website by explaining its content and interactive features, and suggesting actions to accomplish specific goals. This would make the web more accessible especially to seniors, blind users and people with mild cognitive impairment. Specifically, the study examines whether such tools can analyze the source code of a webpage to identify its structure and interactive elements, understand which interactive components are required to support users in achieving their goals, and act effectively as assistive technologies. In addition, the work compares leading tools to assess differences in their effectiveness and behavior in supporting accessible web interaction. The work presents two empirical studies in which four popular LLMCA tools are evaluated on a set of public websites, in order to assess their ability to understand web page structures and interactive components and assist users in their tasks. The evaluation combines qualitative and quantitative measures, focusing on accuracy, completeness, and practical usefulness of the responses.Results show a good degree of pertinent and good-quality answers, even on websites with a poorly accessible structure. The user-friendly way to interact with a LLMCA makes it much comfortable to use for the average user. However, the study also highlights that some LLMCAs appear more 'skilled' in accessibility tasks than others. LLMCAs show promising potential not only to complement existing assistive technologies but also to support or replace the human assistance that is often required for many users to effectively access the web.

items.title: Comparative performance of Chinese and international large language models in patient education on testicular torsion: a cross-sectional study
items.abstract: Background Patients and caregivers increasingly rely on LLMs for health information, yet their performance in TT, a time-critical urological emergency, remains insufficiently characterized. This study compared three LLMs across content safety, quality, reliability, readability, understandability, and actionability. Methods Twenty-five standardized patient-centered questions were developed based on clinical guidelines, expert consensus documents, and information needs identified through Google Trends. Each question was submitted to GPT-5.6 Sol (High reasoning mode), DeepSeek-V4-Pro, and Doubao 2.0 Expert Model, yielding 75 responses. Quality and reliability were assessed using GQS, mDISCERN, and QAMAI; understandability and actionability were evaluated using PEMAT-U and PEMAT-A, respectively. Readability was assessed using six English-language indices, and content deficiencies were also evaluated. Results GPT-5.6 Sol(High reasoning mode) achieved significantly higher GQS, mDISCERN, and QAMAI scores than the other two models (all overall P < 0.001). Hallucinations and factual inaccuracies occurred in 28.0% and 17.3% of responses, respectively. No hallucinations were detected in GPT-5.6 Sol responses, compared with 44.0% for DeepSeek-V4-Pro and 40.0% for Doubao 2.0 Expert Model. Understandability did not differ significantly among models ( P = 0.0735), whereas actionability did ( P < 0.001), with GPT-5.6 Sol(High reasoning mode) performing best. All six readability indices differed significantly among models (all P < 0.001). DeepSeek-V4-Pro showed the most favorable relative readability, GPT-5.6 Sol(High reasoning mode) intermediate performance, and Doubao 2.0 Expert Model the greatest reading difficulty. Conclusions The three LLMs exhibited distinct performance profiles in generating TT-related health information. GPT-5.6 Sol (High reasoning mode) achieved the highest scores for quality, reliability, and actionability, whereas DeepSeek-V4-Pro showed comparatively better readability. Understandability did not differ significantly among models. However, hallucinations, factual inaccuracies, and substantial reading demands remain concerns. These findings reflect model performance under the specific evaluation conditions and at the time of data collection, rather than established clinical effectiveness or safety. GPT-5.6 Sol(High reasoning mode) may be the most suitable supplementary information tool among the models evaluated, but it should not replace professional medical assessment or clinical decision-making.

items.title: Comparing Gamified Biofeedback and Visual Distraction for Acute Pain: Subjective and Psychophysiological Outcomes
items.abstract: Abstract Attentional distraction is an established strategy for reducing acute pain, yet relatively few studies have examined the psychophysiological correlates of gamified biofeedback interventions. This pilot study investigated whether gamified biofeedback tasks can modulate subjective and physiological responses to acute pain. Twenty healthy adults participated in a within-subject experiment consisting of three successive pain conditions, induced by the Cold Pressor Test. The first trial used no intervention, followed by two gamified intervention conditions, presented in a counterbalanced order across participants. One used electrodermal activity (EDA) biofeedback with the Calm The Waves (CTW) system; the other used a visual search task designed to induce cognitive load. Seven participants had prior training in the CTW task (experts). Subjective pain intensity was assessed using a Numeric Rating Scale (NRS), and EDA was continuously recorded throughout each two-minute trial. Mixed-design repeated-measures analyses of variance (ANOVAs) were conducted to examine the effects of condition and prior CTW training. Subjective pain ratings differed significantly across pain conditions, F (2, 36) = 11.41, p < .001, ηp² = .388. Pain baseline M = 6.80 (1.10), pain with CTW M = 6.30 (1.90) and pain with Visual Task M = 5.40 (1.70). In contrast, mean EDA did not differ significantly across conditions, nor across participants’ expertise status. These findings suggest that gamified interventions are associated with reduced subjective pain during acute pain exposure, while corresponding changes in average electrodermal activity were not evident. Both real-time physiological biofeedback and sustained cognitive engagement may contribute to acute pain modulation, although further research is needed to determine whether these effects translate into broader self-regulation skills. Future studies with larger samples and clinical populations should investigate whether dynamic EDA measures are more sensitive indicators of physiological changes associated with acute pain. These findings may contribute to the refinement of biofeedback training approaches for acute pain modulation.

items.title: Comparison of Diagnostic Accuracy of Artificial Intelligence With That of Conventional Diagnostic Methods for Root Fracture Detection: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.abstract: Diagnosing root fractures, especially vertical root fractures (VRFs), is one of the most difficult diagnostic issues in endodontics. Despite the growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in radiograph interpretation, no pooled diagnostic-accuracy estimates have existed for this question. The aim was to systematically review and meta-analyze the diagnostic accuracy of AI for detecting root fractures across cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT), periapical, and panoramic radiography. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Web of Science, Embase, and IEEE Xplore were searched from the date of inception to June 2026 (PROSPERO CRD420251121564). Eligible studies used AI to diagnose root fracture with extractable 2×2 diagnostic data. Risk of bias was assessed with QUADAS-2. Pooled sensitivity and specificity were derived using a bivariate random-effects model with the hierarchical summary receiver operating characteristic (HSROC) modeling. Thirteen studies (2013-2026) were synthesized qualitatively; three (576 fractured, 576 non-fractured teeth) contributed to the meta-analysis. Pooled sensitivity was 0.95 (95% confidence interval (CI): 0.90-0.97), and pooled specificity was 0.97 (95% CI: 0.77-1.00). Heterogeneity was substantial for sensitivity (I²=77.9%) and specificity (I²=95.6%), driven largely by one outlying study. The summary point approximated the ideal upper-left corner of SROC space. Certainty of evidence was moderate. AI demonstrated excellent pooled diagnostic accuracy for root-fracture detection, with CBCT-based deep learning models performing best. However, substantial heterogeneity and risk-of-bias concerns temper confidence, pending larger, prospective, externally validated studies.

items.title: Comparison of Horizontal and Vertical Tonovet Plus Clinical Measurement Configurations for Intraocular Pressure Assessment in Conscious Cats
items.abstract: Rebound tonometry is widely used for measuring intraocular pressure (IOP) in cats; however, differences in clinical tonometer measurement configuration may contribute to variability in recorded values. This prospective repeated-measures study compared IOP measurements obtained using horizontal and vertical Tonovet Plus clinical measurement configurations in 32 client-owned, systemically and ophthalmologically normal conscious cats. Intraocular pressure was measured in the right eye while the probe was directed toward the center of the cornea and positioned 4-8 mm from the corneal surface. The order of horizontal and vertical configurations was randomized for each cat. Measurements were obtained by one experienced veterinary ophthalmologist and a trained student operator group. In the primary linear mixed-effects analysis accounting for repeated measurements within cats, horizontal configuration was associated with an estimated 2.41-mmHg higher IOP than vertical configuration (β = 2.41 mmHg; 95% CI, 1.39-3.44; p < 0.001). The configuration-associated difference was also observed separately for the experienced instructor (mean difference, 2.81 mmHg; 95% CI, 1.91-3.71; p < 0.001) and across the trained student operator group (2.00 mmHg; 95% CI, 0.81-3.19; p = 0.002). These findings indicate that horizontal and vertical Tonovet Plus clinical measurement configurations may yield different IOP values in conscious cats. As configuration changes may affect instrument handling, restraint, head positioning, and animal responses, the difference cannot be attributed solely to tonometer orientation or mechanics. Consistent configuration is therefore recommended when comparing serial IOP measurements in cats. Further controlled studies are needed to distinguish mechanical, ergonomic, and other examination-related mechanisms.

items.title: Compiler.next: A Search-Based Compiler to Power the AI-Native Future of Software Engineering
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of AI-assisted software engineering has brought transformative potential to the field of software engineering, but existing tools and paradigms remain limited by cognitive overload, inefficient tool integration, and the narrow capabilities of AI copilots. In response, we propose Compiler.next , a novel search-based compiler designed to enable the seamless evolution of AI-native software systems as part of the emerging Software Engineering 3.0 era. Unlike traditional static compilers, Compiler.next takes human-written intents and automatically generates working software by searching for an optimal solution. This process involves dynamic optimization of cognitive architectures and their constituents (e.g., prompts, foundation model configurations, and system parameters) while finding the optimal tradeoff between several objectives, such as accuracy, cost, and latency. This article outlines the architecture of Compiler.next and positions it as a cornerstone in democratizing software development by lowering the technical barrier for non-experts, enabling scalable, adaptable, and reliable AI-powered software. We present a roadmap to address the core challenges in intent compilation, including developing quality programming constructs, effective search heuristics, reproducibility, and interoperability between compilers. Our vision lays the groundwork for fully automated, search-driven software development, fostering faster innovation and more efficient AI-driven systems.

This monograph formalizes Complexity and Information Compression Dynamics (CICD) as a substrate-invariant theoretical framework governing the joint evolution of structural coordination overhead and cross-boundary information compression. Every bounded system operates on a finite flux of gross capacity (E_gross) partitioned between internal maintenance and coordination overhead (E_maint) and net discretionary surplus (E_net). Because relational interdependencies scale super-linearly with effective structural dimensionality (C), every non-modular topology encounters a hard thermodynamic ceiling—the Complexity Maximum (C_max)—where internal upkeep consumes total capacity (E_net → 0). Simultaneously, transmitting high-dimensional internal states across finite-bandwidth internal or external interfaces (B_int) requires lossy compression, elevating the dimensionless Information Compression Friction Index (Φ ≥ 1) above the Landauer–Shannon thermodynamic floor and inflicting structural fidelity loss (ΔΨ). items.title: Conceptual Framework for a Virtual Symbiotic Environment for Maritime Operations Using Digital Twins and Explainable Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Digital Twin technologies in maritime applications have primarily focused on individual subsystems, such as vessel machinery, navigation, or environmental monitoring, while limited attention has been given to the integrated representation of human operators, vessel dynamics, machinery, and environmental conditions. To address this challenge, a conceptual Virtual Symbiotic Environment for Maritime Operations (VSEMO) is proposed; the VSEMO integrates human, traffic, docking, environmental, and machinery Digital Twins within a closed-loop system engineering framework. The proposed architecture incorporates Explainable Artificial Intelligence to support transparent operational risk assessment and decision support, while immersive virtual reality provides a realistic environment for adaptive operator training. As an initial proof of concept, a Graph Convolutional Network is developed using synthetic graph-based operational scenarios to demonstrate the feasibility of jointly estimating subsystem-level and aggregate operational risk indicators. Although the computational implementation is limited to snapshot-based synthetic data, the proposed framework establishes a scalable and modular foundation for future real-time Digital Twin ecosystems that integrate physiological sensing, vessel telemetry, environmental information, and explainable artificial intelligence for maritime training and decision support.

items.title: Constituting Technological Stigma: The Oscillating Stigmatization of Internal Combustion Engine Scooters
items.abstract: Technologies can themselves become objects of stigmatization, rather than merely serving as vehicles through which stigma is directed at associated individuals or organizations. As technologies evolve, shifts in their benefits and harms may alter the grounds for stigma. Yet it remains unclear how these shifts shape stigma trajectories. We examine this issue through a longitudinal qualitative study of the stigmatization of internal combustion engine (ICE) scooters in Taiwan (2009–2021), a case in which a proposal to phase them out in favor of electric scooters was later withdrawn. We show how stigmatizing and stigmatized audiences, evolving technologies, and infrastructures co-constitute evaluative conditions that shape which attributes and consequences acquire discrediting significance. Stigma first attached to legacy ICE models and then spread to all ICE scooters. Its scope later narrowed as upgraded variants regained acceptance, although legacy models remained discredited. This oscillating trajectory unfolds through three mechanisms: constituting a graded technological order, polarizing this order, and reconstituting technological normality. Our model thus extends audience-centered accounts by explaining how human and nonhuman elements jointly shape the trajectory and scope of technology stigma.

items.title: Construction of Reliable Vertical Large Language Model Systems for Sustainable Catalysis: From Evidence‐Bound Knowledge Extraction to Closed‐Loop Catalyst Discovery
items.abstract: Catalysis is central to energy conversion and green chemistry, but its development is constrained by fragmented literature data, complex reaction systems, difficult mechanistic identification, and reliance on empirical trial and error. Large language models (LLMs), with capabilities in unstructured text understanding, multisource knowledge integration, reasoning, and tool invocation, have been increasingly applied to literature extraction, characterization analysis, mechanistic hypothesis generation, catalyst recommendation, condition optimization, and automated experimentation. However, catalytic tasks are highly specialized, condition-dependent, and validation-intensive, making general-purpose LLMs insufficient for traceable, verifiable, safe, and controllable research. This review summarizes recent progress in applying LLMs to key catalytic tasks and discusses their reliability requirements. We further propose a catalysis-oriented vertical LLM framework consisting of "task definition-evidence access-constraint control-model adaptation-validation evaluation-feedback updating." By integrating evidence-constrained knowledge extraction, constraint-aware decision-making, and feedback-driven closed-loop optimization, this framework aims to reduce low-value trial-and-error experiments, unnecessary reagent consumption, energy input, and waste generation, thereby supporting reliable and sustainable catalysis research.

items.title: Contesting sociotechnical imaginaries: the technopolitics of artificial intelligence/cybersecurity convergence
items.abstract: Abstract The current development of artificial intelligence (AI) is sustained by powerful imaginaries that describe possible technological futures aligning with the normative preferences of influential actors. We show how an AI imaginary driven by “Big Tech” corporate interests and technosolutionism has influenced the development of an AI/cybersecurity imaginary in the UK. Building on the Science and Technology Studies concept of sociotechnical imaginaries, we adopt atechnopolitical lens to examine how external notions of AI progress and development interacted with internal U.K. government commitments to cybersecurity. Drawing on U.K. government texts and interviews with 37 officials, nongovernment experts, and industry actors, we trace the emergence of an AI/cybersecurity imaginary between 2022 and 2024, how intragovernment controversies were negotiated and resolved, and how this imaginary stabilised in U.K. security politics with identifiable outcomes in cybersecurity governance. The article contributes empirical support for the importance of sociotechnical imaginaries in understanding security trajectories, how corporate and technosolutionist imaginaries influence government policy and practice, and offer theoretical insights into the dynamics of imaginary formation and function. AI imaginaries promote the goals and values of science and technology, while technopolitics dominated by corporate actors and technoscientific optimism constrain governmental and social capacity to create and enact alternative imaginaries of future cybersecurity.

items.title: Conventional and Digital Prosthetic Appliances in Cleft Lip and Palate Care: A Scoping Review
items.abstract: Cleft lip and palate (CL/P) are congenital craniofacial conditions that require coordinated, multidisciplinary care from infancy through growth. Presurgical orthopedic and prosthetic appliances, such as feeding/palatal plates and nasoalveolar molding (NAM) devices, are used in selected patients, and digital workflows based on intraoral or three-dimensional (3D) scanning, computer-aided design and manufacturing (CAD/CAM), and 3D printing are increasingly proposed as alternatives to conventional fabrication. This study was conducted to map the available evidence on conventionally and digitally fabricated prosthetic and presurgical appliances for infants and young children with CL/P, to describe the characteristics of that evidence, and to identify research gaps. A scoping review was conducted and reported according to the PRISMA extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR), using a Population–Concept–Context framework. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, and Google Scholar were searched. Two reviewers screened records independently. Data were charted using a predefined set of items and summarized descriptively (counts and percentages) and narratively. No formal risk-of-bias assessment or meta-analysis was undertaken. Thirty sources were included: 7 systematic reviews (3 with meta-analysis), 1 randomized controlled trial, 2 observational clinical studies, 13 case reports, case series, or technical reports, 4 workflow-development or technical-validation studies, 2 in vitro studies, and 1 narrative review. Twenty-three sources (76.7%) were published in 2021 or later. By focus, 10 addressed feeding/palatal plates and obturators, 4 digital impression or scanning, 5 conventional NAM, 9 digital NAM or presurgical plate workflows, and 2 artificial intelligence (AI)-supported planning. Digital workflows were feasible in all categories and offered advantages in data storage, reproducibility, and virtual adjustment. Improved fit was demonstrated mainly in vitro. The only randomized trial in neonates (n = 30) favored digital over tray impressions, whereas a meta-analysis of five randomized trials found no significant differences between digital and conventional NAM in several presurgical outcomes, with low-to-moderate certainty of evidence. Digital workflows redistributed rather than uniformly reduced work time. Digital technology should be regarded as an extension of established clinical practice rather than an automatic substitute for conventional methods. The evidence base is recent, small, and dominated by low-level designs. Future progress depends on standardized digital protocols, larger randomized trials, long-term follow-up, validated materials, and careful integration of AI with clinical expertise.

items.title: Crisis Governance at the Joints. Mapping the Ethical and Societal Territory of Crisis Management Technologies: The Case of Human-Swarm Teaming
items.abstract: Crisis and disaster governance increasingly relies on technologies that sense, classify and act faster than humans can. Drone swarms coordinated with human operators, known as human-swarm teaming, provide a productive case to review the field of crisis governance. They promise better situational awareness in disaster response, but they also raise questions about human control, responsibility, surveillance, triage, dual use and public legitimacy. This report maps the ethical and societal territory that HST opens up. It unpacks this territory with a 3i-framework, the Interface, where operators and swarms work together, the Infrastructure, where organisations distribute tasks, decisions and blame, and the Imaginary, where law, policy and shared societal assumptions define what a crisis is and which interventions it justifies. The central claim is that these concerns cannot be addressed one level at a time. Many of the most pressing problems, such as responsibility gaps and the erosion of meaningful human control, arise at the joints between levels, through four translations, habits harden, routines become stories, principles become procedures, and procedures become prompts. Drawing on a critical review of literature across philosophy of technology, political theory, moral psychology, philosophy of mind, AI ethics, and critical disaster and security studies, the report develops this framework, illustrates it with two worked examples, and derives design and governance implications and a set of questions for developers, emergency organisations and policymakers.

items.title: Cross-domain encoding models reveal shared and domain-specific neural representations across language and mathematics
items.abstract: Whether language and mathematics rely on shared or distinct neural representations remains unresolved in cognitive neuroscience. Here, we combined latent features from a large language model with functional magnetic resonance imaging encoding models to test cross-domain generalization in 32 participants performing sentence comprehension and calculation tasks. Cross-domain prediction identified cortical regions showing partially shared representations, most consistently in the left area 55b, while control analyses suggested that these effects could not be fully explained by low-level visual or task-general factors. Domain-specificity contrasts revealed stronger language-related prediction in the left superior temporal sulcus and angular gyrus and math-related prediction in the left precentral sulcus and bilateral intraparietal sulci. Model-weight analyses revealed distinct weight profiles associated with shared and domain-specific prediction patterns. Cross-domain regions also exhibited task-dependent functional coupling with language- and math-related networks. Together, these findings suggest that language and mathematics involve partially shared neural representations alongside domain-specific cortical organization, helping reconcile previous contrasting views on their neural basis.

items.title: Cuando trabajar enferma: incumplimiento de normas de seguridad y salud laboral y sus consecuencias en el bienestar de los trabajadores
items.abstract: La existencia de normas de seguridad y salud laboral no garantiza que los riesgos ocupacionales estén efectivamente controlados. El objetivo fue analizar críticamente la evidencia sobre cumplimiento preventivo, exposición ocupacional y bienestar de los trabajadores, y formular un marco integrado de evaluación. Se realizó una revisión narrativa crítica mediante búsquedas web dirigidas a publicaciones académicas y fuentes institucionales, con verificación de metadatos en registros bibliográficos y sitios oficiales. Se seleccionaron veinte documentos por su pertinencia, diferenciando investigaciones, síntesis de evidencia y orientaciones técnicas. Los hallazgos muestran que determinadas inspecciones pueden reducir lesiones, que las condiciones laborales adversas se relacionan con problemas de salud física y mental y que la documentación resulta insuficiente para valorar la protección efectiva. La relación entre exposición y enfermedad no demuestra por sí sola incumplimiento jurídico ni permite atribuirle toda la carga de daño. Se propone un marco que distingue requisitos aplicables, controles operativos, exposición y resultados de salud, con participación de los trabajadores y seguimiento correctivo. Se concluye que la evaluación preventiva necesita integrar evidencia documental, condiciones reales de trabajo y bienestar. El alcance narrativo, el acceso desigual a textos completos y la ausencia de datos propios limitan la inferencia causal y la transferencia local.

items.title: Cultivating Effective Reading Habits in Higher Education: Challenges and Pathways to English Language Proficiency
items.abstract: Reading plays a fundamental role in the development of English language proficiency by enhancing vocabulary acquisition, grammatical knowledge, comprehension abilities, and critical thinking skills. Despite its importance, many university students encounter persistent challenges that hinder the development of effective reading habits and limit opportunities for meaningful language growth. This paper examines the major barriers affecting reading development among university students and explores how these challenges influence English language proficiency. Guided by Reading Engagement Theory and Self-Determination Theory, the discussion is organised around four interconnected dimensions: cognitive and affective barriers to reading development, reading culture and literacy support, literacy competence and advanced reading challenges, and pedagogical practices influencing reading engagement. The analysis suggests that reading anxiety, limited intrinsic motivation, dependence on extrinsic incentives, inadequate literacy support, vocabulary limitations, weak critical reading skills, and traditional instructional approaches collectively restrict students' reading development. Furthermore, excessive reliance on passive learning strategies and fragmented vocabulary instruction may impede learners' ability to engage deeply with texts and develop higher-order comprehension skills. The paper argues that successful reading development requires more than exposure to texts alone; it demands supportive learning environments, meaningful reading experiences, learner autonomy, and instructional approaches that promote active engagement. Strengthening reading culture, expanding opportunities for extensive reading, and fostering intrinsic motivation may contribute significantly to improved language proficiency and academic achievement. Future research should explore digital reading environments, reading engagement in multilingual contexts, technology-assisted literacy development, and the long-term effects of reading habits on language learning outcomes.

items.title: Cultural Bias and Representational Gaps in Conversational Generative AI for Mental Health: A Systematic Review
items.abstract: Limited access to mental health support due to infrastructural limitations and workforce shortages has contributed to growing interest in the use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) for scalable mental health support. Despite their promise, these technologies pose risks, such as hallucinations and misalignment with local experiences of mental health challenges in the Global South. While there is growing attention to safety and harm mitigation, limited research has examined how cultural representation, linguistic coverage, and dataset provenance shape these technologies, particularly for Global South populations, and how cultural sensitivity can be improved to support mental health care. This systematic review synthesises 29 empirical studies published between 2020 and April 2026, predominantly concerning conversational GenAI for mental health. Using a keyword-based search strategy, critical narrative synthesis, and reflexive deductive thematic analysis, we examined how GenAI systems encode cultural assumptions. Our findings reveal representational gaps, limited culturally grounded narratives, and predominantly additive adaptation, whereby cultural elements are introduced while underlying Western diagnostic and therapeutic frameworks generally remain unchanged. Also, we consolidate cross-study evidence into strategies that have implications for clinical and non-clinical collaborative practices for mental health support. Lastly, we outline implications for Human-Centred AI and Computer-Supported Cooperative Work and directions for culturally grounded conversational GenAI that supports equitable mental health care.

items.title: Curriculum–Industry Alignment in Civil Engineering Education in the Philippines: Perspectives of Graduates and Construction Industry Practitioners on Competency Gaps and Future Workforce Needs
items.abstract: The rapid transformation of the construction industry driven by digitalization, sustainability requirements, and evolving project delivery methods has increased the need for civil engineering curricula that are responsive to industry demands. This study evaluated the alignment between civil engineering education and construction-industry requirements by comparing the perspectives of civil engineering graduates and industry practitioners. A cross-sectional descriptive-comparative research design was employed involving 127 respondents, consisting of 79 civil engineering graduates with less than three years of professional experience and 48 industry practitioners with more than three years of construction-related experience. Data were collected using a researcher-developed questionnaire covering four dimensions: curriculum relevance and adequacy, observed competency deficiencies, preparedness for emerging technologies and practices, and recommended curricular reforms. Descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, Mann–Whitney U tests, weighted ranking analysis, and thematic analysis were performed. The instrument demonstrated excellent reliability, with Cronbach’s alpha values ranging from 0.914 to 0.959. Results indicated that both graduates and industry practitioners perceived the current curriculum as insufficiently aligned with contemporary construction-industry needs and identified competency gaps primarily related to construction software proficiency, planning and scheduling, contract administration, and site supervision. Although respondents considered the curriculum to provide moderate preparation for emerging technologies, substantial gaps remained in areas such as Building Information Modeling (BIM), digital construction tools, artificial intelligence, data analytics, and reality-capture technologies. No statistically significant differences were observed between graduates and industry practitioners across the four assessment dimensions (p > 0.05), indicating a strong consensus regarding curriculum strengths, deficiencies, and future priorities. Internship and industry immersion programs, construction planning and scheduling, industry-based case studies, software training, and BIM education emerged as the highest-priority curricular reforms. The findings highlight the need for a more industry-responsive and technology-oriented civil engineering curriculum that strengthens experiential learning, digital competencies, and industry engagement to better prepare graduates for the evolving demands of the construction sector.

items.title: CyDeBoost: A SHAP-Guided Boosting Strategy Framework for Cyberbullying Detection through Mistake-Driven Learning
items.abstract: The widespread use of online social media has increased the urgency of detecting and mitigating harmful language, such as cyberbullying. Traditional detection systems often struggle with semantically ambiguous and context-dependent expressions, leading to frequent misclassifications. This article presents CyDeBoost, a mistake-driven boosting framework for cyberbullying detection. The core idea of CyDeBoost is to identify and learn from misclassified instances by leveraging SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) to uncover key lexical features responsible for prediction errors. Based on these insights, the framework uses large language models to generate semantically contrastive augmented samples, which are then used to fine-tune the model through a modular continual learning strategy. Specifically, lightweight adapter modules are stacked iteratively to simulate the boosting process while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Experimental results demonstrate that CyDeBoost improves classification robustness across multiple cyberbullying categories and maintains generalization under low-resource settings. This framework aligns with the goals of content moderation on dynamic web platforms by offering interpretable, adaptive, and resource-efficient language safety solutions.

items.title: Data-Intensive and Ai-Mediated Anticipatory Governance: A Functional Typology of Institutional Capacity, Decision-Making, and Governance of Expertise
items.abstract: Abstract Anticipatory Governance (AG) has emerged as a strategic approach for addressing uncertainty, systemic risk, and complexity in contemporary socio-technical systems. Governments and universities increasingly rely on Big Data, Data Science, and Artificial Intelligence (AI) to support future-oriented public decision-making, yet the institutional and societal implications of these technologies remain conceptually fragmented. This article addresses this gap through a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) that examines how data-intensive and AI-enabled capabilities become embedded across foresight, knowledge creation, policy design, and policy assessment. Rather than treating the generic technical differences among Big Data, Data Science, and AI as the principal contribution, the study develops a functional typology that distinguishes infrastructural observation and evidentiary integration, analytical modeling and interpretation, and AI-enabled decision mediation. The review analyzes how these functions respond to uncertainty, non-linearity, interdependence, and feedback; reshape informational, analytical, and decisional capacity; and redistribute epistemic and decisional authority. The findings indicate a cumulative but non-deterministic movement from expanded observability, to analytical structuring, to increasingly mediated action. We conceptualize this movement as decisional embedding: the degree to which technological systems enter the institutional production of alternatives, prioritization, recommendation, adjustment, or execution. The contribution lies in showing that technological integration in anticipatory governance is not merely an increase in computational capability, but a reconfiguration of knowledge, judgment, responsibility, and authority. The article concludes with implications for accountable, contestable, and human-governed hybrid decision architectures.

items.title: Decision Considerations Influencing Information Systems Modularity: A Multimethod Study of LEGO
items.abstract: Abstract. The maturing of concepts such as microservices and open application programming interfaces (APIs) has radically increased the practicality of fine-grained modularization in Information Systems (IS) architecture. These are critical technical advancements, given the central role of modularity in the ability of IS to transform and meet future organizational needs efficiently. Nevertheless, reports from practice suggest that, when presented with new opportunities for modularization, organizations face multifaceted decision criteria and do not necessarily embrace new approaches as may be expected. While emergent IS literature observes that organizations’ decisions on modularity in IS may involve competing concerns, understanding of the considerations involved and how they influence such decisions remains limited. To examine these considerations, we intensively study the experience of LEGO, a global toy company. Specifically, we sequentially apply multiple methods consisting of an exploratory inductive analysis of LEGO’s approach to IS modularity decisions over 36 months, which then informs a crisp-set qualitative comparative analysis (QCA) of 31 episodes of LEGO’s situated decision-making on IS modularity. Through the analysis, we find the rationale for a purposeful choice between two forms of modularity that differ in granularity of decomposition, rather than a linear pursuit of maximizing decomposability in IS architecture. We bring to the fore a perspective of IS modularity as situated decisions reconciling competing demands in pursuit of the right type of modularity, in the right place to achieve the right effect. Our findings add nuance to modularity in the context of IS architecture and explain the complex causality of IS modularity decisions.

items.title: Depth-Gated Evidence Availability: How a Search Can Miss the Evidence Needed to Widen It
items.abstract: This conceptual paper introduces Depth-Gated Evidence Availability, a mechanism through which the scope of a diagnosis determines what evidence an inquiry can obtain. An investigator who treats a model’s assumptions as settled can test different values within it while leaving those assumptions unexamined. This creates a particular difficulty when the evidence that would justify widening the inquiry depends on a comparison that the current inquiry has no occasion to make. The paper assesses a choice of diagnostic depth by asking what questions the current frame permits, what evidence would bear on a deeper alternative, and whether the present investigation could obtain it. To identify the mechanism, one must trace a specific gap in the evidence to a question the frame excludes and show how asking that question makes the evidence obtainable. A narrow investigation can still be proportionate to its purpose. The value and cost of the missing comparison matter when deciding whether to pursue it. The paper places the mechanism alongside Thomas Kuhn’s account of how paradigms guide the selection of scientific problems and examines two historical cases. In 1901, the Wright brothers’ glider produced about one-third of the lift they expected. Their wind tunnel allowed them to compare different wing shapes under the same conditions. The comparison supported Lilienthal’s measurements for his own wing and exposed a problem in applying them to the Wrights’ wings. In 1909, Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden asked whether alpha particles could return from a metal surface. A screen shielded from direct particles let them observe returns that earlier forward measurements could not register. Those observations later informed Ernest Rutherford’s proposal of a concentrated central charge. Part of the Recursive Inquiry and Encounter series within On Human Modeling, the paper has a potential application in human–AI evaluation. Reviewers who vary a prompt and score each answer may take for granted that the assistant received the relevant source passage. Asking which passages actually reached the assistant calls for a different record. That record lets reviewers distinguish a passage the system omitted from one it received and failed to use.

items.title: Design Science Research, Co-Creation, and User-Centred Design: Foundations for Developing Responsible Digital Health Solutions for Chronic Disease Management
items.abstract: The rapid evolution of digital health technologies—including artificial intelligence (AI), mobile health (mHealth), wearable sensors, digital therapeutics, and intelligent decision support systems—has transformed opportunities for supporting individuals living with chronic diseases such as diabetes and asthma. However, technological sophistication alone does not guarantee successful adoption or meaningful health outcomes. Many digital health interventions fail because they are designed around technology rather than people, inadequately consider clinical workflows, neglect socio-cultural contexts, or overlook ethical and governance considerations. This chapter argues that responsible digital health innovation requires integrating three complementary methodological approaches: Design Science Research (DSR), co-creation, and user-centred design (UCD). Together, these approaches enable the development of clinically useful, ethically responsible, technically robust, and socially acceptable digital health solutions. The chapter examines the theoretical foundations of each methodology, demonstrates how they complement one another throughout the innovation lifecycle, and illustrates their application through examples from diabetes and asthma management. A practical framework is presented that integrates DSR, co-creation, and UCD into a continuous cycle of problem identification, iterative development, evaluation, implementation, and responsible innovation.

items.title: Designing the dialogue: A participatory study to develop AI-mediated architecture critiques
items.abstract: The pedagogy of the Architecture Design studio centers on iterative learning and critique, yet traditional review formats often induce information overload and psychosocial barriers for students. Concurrently, while artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in architectural education, its application remains largely instrumentcentric, acting as an assistant for early-stage ideation and technical optimization.This instrument-centric approach neglects AI's potential to support higher-order cognitive tasks and risks fostering passive learning. To address this gap, this study investigates how Large Language Models (LLMs) can be repositioned as active "reflection partners" to mitigate the social pressure of critiques and scaffold objective, self-regulated learning across individual self-reflection, peer-to-peer critique, and professor-led critique. Using Participatory Design (PD) methodology, this study engaged 22 architecture students in a series of co-design workshops. Participants engaged in structured ideation and created low-fidelity, paper-based wireframes simulating AI-mediated interactions. The collected artifacts and sticky-note rationales were evaluated using reflexive thematic analysis. The findings reveal that students prioritize human-centered AI features that safeguard personal agency, including robust anonymity controls, intent-alignment checking to prevent AI from becoming a rigid evaluator, and multi-stakeholder role-playing simulations. These insights informed the conceptualization of "Studioboard, " a proposed LLM-integrated platform that synthesizes peer and professor critique, translates complex terminology, and tracks curriculum-level progress over time. The study concludes that user-designed, AI-mediated critique platforms can effectively neutralize the power hierarchies and social anxieties inherent in architectural reviews.

items.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Coastal zones worldwide are increasingly vulnerable to climate-induced hazards, with coastal flooding emerging as one of the most pressing environmental threats. Rising sea levels, intensified storm surges, and changing precipitation patterns driven by climate change pose significant risks to populations, infrastructure, and ecosystems. Geospatial Artificial Intelligence (GeoAI) an integration of geospatial analytics and machine learning using Google Earth Engine (GEE) to enhance the accuracy of flood risk prediction in selected Nigerian coastal zones. METHOD: This study employed a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) guided by the PRISMA framework to examine the application of AI-powered geo-spatial models for predicting subsurface instability and enhancing infrastructure resilience in Nigeria’s coastal and flood-prone regions. Relevant studies from 2000–2022 were sourced from major academic databases using defined inclusion and exclusion criteria. A thematic content analysis revealed key trends, challenges, and innovations in applying AI and geospatial intelligence to risk prediction and resilience planning. Findings highlight the importance of integrating AI-driven geo-spatial modelling for adaptive urban planning and sustainable infrastructure management in climate-vulnerable environments. FINDINGS: This research demonstrates the potential of AI-powered geospatial modeling to support data-driven climate adaptation and sustainable flood management in Nigeria’s vulnerable coastal environments. A composite flood susceptibility model was developed by integrating distance, elevation, vegetation, and moisture indices, producing a detailed flood hazard map that categorizes risk levels from very low to very high. The results show enhanced interpretation and decision-making. Overall, the findings demonstrate the effectiveness of AI-driven geospatial modeling in identifying and visualizing flood-prone areas for informed planning and disaster risk reduction. DISCUSSION: The study demonstrates the significant potential of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and geo-spatial modeling in detecting subsurface instability and predicting flood hazards in Nigeria’s coastal regions. By integrating multi-source datasets within Google Earth Engine (GEE) and applying advanced machine learning algorithms such as Random Forest, SVM, and Neural Networks, and revealed that low-lying, moisture-rich, and poorly vegetated areas exhibit the highest flood susceptibility. Embedding AI-powered geospatial analytics into planning frameworks can transform flood management from reactive to proactive, fostering resilient infrastructure, sustainable development, and climate adaptation in Nigeria’s vulnerable coastal regions.

items.title: Digital Ecosystems and Social Media for Student Well-Being and Resilience in Higher Education
items.abstract: This chapter examines the dynamic interplay between digital environments and student psychological well-being in higher education. Conceptualising universities as active ecosystems in which personal trajectories interact with structural determinants, it uses a narrative synthesis to connect empirical research on psychological outcomes with institutional policy. The theoretical framework integrates Neo-Ecological theory, including virtual microsystems and artificial intelligence, with Self-Determination Theory and cognitive-behavioural models. The analysis addresses systemic stressors such as technostress and metadata encroachment, alongside protective factors including social capital and smart learning. By identifying policy gaps between technology integration and privacy governance, this chapter proposes strengthening emotional infrastructure and digital resilience. Ultimately, it offers a roadmap for transitioning higher education institutions to develop sustainable, preventive campus cultures aligned with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals.

items.title: Digital Health Literacy and Verification of Sexual and Reproductive Health Information on TikTok: The Role of Artificial Intelligence Among Young People in Timor-Leste
items.abstract: Abstract Social media platforms, particularly TikTok, have become increasingly important sources of health information among young people. However, the accuracy of health-related content remains a concern, especially regarding sexual and reproductive health (SRH). The ability to evaluate online information and verify its credibility is therefore an essential component of digital health literacy. The emergence of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools, such as ChatGPT and Google Gemini, also provides new opportunities for users to seek additional explanations and verify health-related information. Nevertheless, the reliability of AI-generated responses requires critical evaluation. This study aims to examine digital health literacy and the verification of sexual and reproductive health information encountered on TikTok among young people in Timor-Leste, with particular attention to the use of AI tools. An analytical cross-sectional study will be conducted among young people aged 18–24 years who use TikTok in Timor-Leste. The study will target 200 respondents using a non-probability convenience sampling technique. Data will be collected through a structured, self-administered online questionnaire using Google Forms. The questionnaire will assess TikTok exposure to SRH information, trust in health-related content, information verification practices, digital health literacy, and the use of AI tools for health information verification. Data will be analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics to examine patterns of information verification and relationships among the study variables. The study is expected to provide evidence on how young people evaluate and verify SRH information encountered on TikTok and how AI tools contribute to their information-seeking practices. The findings may support the development of digital health literacy initiatives and promote responsible use of AI for health information among young people in Timor-Leste.

items.title: Digital Transformation and Pandemic Resilience in Global Logistics: A Comparative Case Analysis of DHL's Supply Chain Operations in the United Kingdom and United States
items.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic exposed structural fragilities in global supply chains and accelerated logistics providers' investment in digital technology. This paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI), blockchain, and the Internet of Things (IoT) have contributed to pandemic resilience in global logistics, using DHL's operations in the United Kingdom and the United States as an illustrative comparative case. Drawing on industry reports, trade-body surveys, and the academic literature, the analysis finds that these technologies strengthen supply chain visibility, forecasting capability, and transactional trust, while high implementation costs, legacy-system integration, and cybersecurity exposure remain persistent constraints, particularly for smaller operators. A comparison of national contexts suggests that the UK and the US are converging on similar technologies but for different underlying reasons: UK adoption is shaped substantially by post-Brexit uncertainty and shifting consumer behaviour, while US adoption is driven by competition for global technology leadership and by workforce skills shortages. The paper argues that digital investment alone does not guarantee resilience; it must be accompanied by leadership, workforce development, and a long-term strategic orientation toward risk.

items.title: Dino-cd:marrying DINOv3 with dual-branch complementary reconstruction for remote sensing change detection
items.abstract: Abstract The goal of remote sensing change detection (RSCD) is to accurately distinguish land-surface changes. Recently, Vision foundation models (VFMs), such as the self-supervised DINOv3, have demonstrated strong semantic parsing capabilities across various visual tasks. However, directly applying DINOv3 to RSCD remains challenging. First, DINOv3 produces low-resolution, single-scale feature representations, which are unfavorable for pixel-wise change classification. Second, DINOv3 is not tailored for RSCD and thus struggles to model geospatial differences along the temporal dimension. To address these issues, Marrying DINOv3 with Dual-Branch Complementary Reconstruction for Remote Sensing Change Detection (DINO-CD) is proposed. Specifically, a dual-branch complementary reconstruction module is introduced to enable interaction between DINO and CNN branches for complementary feature enhancement, producing multi-scale representations that preserve global semantic consistency while strengthening local detail discrimination. In addition, a hierarchical difference aggregation module is designed to comprehensively enhance temporal discrepancies via explicit frequency learning and multi-scale directional aggregation, thereby highlighting effective change regions and reducing false alarms and missed detections. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate that DINO-CD outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving gains of 6% in F1-score and 8% in IoU on the CLCD dataset.

items.title: Early feedback elicitation and downstream participation behaviours: a retrospective observational analysis of study completion and disengagement
items.abstract: Background Many health research studies and clinical trials face threats to external validity and low statistical power because they are unable to recruit and retain a sufficient number of participants. Identifying study design improvements using participant feedback is an important avenue through which studies seek to address these challenges. However, the returns on this approach have been limited because experience measures are rarely linked to actual participation behaviour. We examine whether feedback collected at the beginning of a research study can provide a meaningful signal about future participation as measured by study completion, withdrawal, and communication unsubscription. Methods We use observational data from a large health research program (N = 35,838; 77% from groups historically underrepresented in biomedical research, UBR) in which feedback was collected across the participant experience. We correlate feedback responses (e.g., indicating satisfaction with the experience) with study completion and active disengagement 6 months later and use Artificial Intelligence (AI) processing of free-text comments to surface specific topics and sentiment. Findings Ratings given immediately after onboarding are associated with an 8.89 percentage-point (pp) higher study completion rate (‘Good' vs ‘Fair') and a 23.22 pp higher active disengagement rate (‘Poor' vs ‘Fair') within 6 months. Associations for feedback collected later are smaller (up to 4.17 pp for completion). These differences hold after adjusting for participant characteristics (age, income, educational attainment, sex at birth, UBR on race/ethnicity, and UBR on rurality). We find no statistically significant effect of the prompt itself. AI-extracted topics and sentiment agree with human reviewers 86% and 81% of the time, respectively. Interpretation Early, light-touch feedback can meaningfully differentiate participants by their likelihood of completing or disengaging from a study, creating opportunities to target support and address flagged concerns while the study is still in progress. Feedback collected at the end of a study is a weaker signal of future behaviour. Our approach, including AI processing of free-text comments, is readily portable to other studies and feedback elicitations. Whether feedback-informed changes improve retention is an important question for future work. Funding National Institutes of Health.

items.title: Eco-AI: Artificial Intelligence Framework for Predicting and Reducing Carbon Emissions in Depok City
items.abstract: Depok City faces increasing carbon emissions associated with rapid urbanization, a population exceeding 2.7 million, and more than 821,000 registered motor vehicles. However, the city lacks an integrated, data-driven framework for predicting greenhouse gas emissions and evaluating emission reduction strategies. This study aimed to develop Eco-AI, an artificial intelligence (AI)-based framework designed to predict greenhouse gas emissions and assess mitigation strategies in Depok City through the integration of multiple predictive and optimization models. A mixed-methods approach was employed, combining quantitative and qualitative analyses using Internet of Things (IoT) sensor measurements (MQ-135 and SDS011), Sentinel-5P satellite observations, and administrative data from relevant government agencies, including DLHK, Dishub, PLN, and BPS. Five AI models were incorporated: long short-term memory (LSTM) networks for time-series forecasting, random forest (RF) for identifying influential emission-related factors, extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) for emission hotspot classification, graph neural networks (GNNs) for spatial analysis, and reinforcement learning using proximal policy optimization (PPO) for policy scenario optimization. The results indicated that Depok City's total greenhouse gas emissions reached 4,217,340 metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent (tCO?e) in 2024, with transportation accounting for 43.2% and residential energy consumption contributing 29.9%. The LSTM model achieved strong predictive performance (R² = 0.924; mean absolute percentage error [MAPE] = 4.97%), while the RF model identified the number of motor vehicles as the most influential predictor (feature importance = 0.234). Under the business-as-usual (BAU) scenario, annual emissions were projected to reach 5,891,200 tCO?e by 2030. The combined mitigation scenario indicated a potential emissions reduction of 19.1% relative to the BAU projection, with an estimated investment requirement of IDR 1.24 trillion. These findings suggested that the Eco-AI framework could support data-driven emissions forecasting, identification of emission-related factors, spatial assessment, and evaluation of mitigation strategies. The framework may contribute to evidence-based urban climate planning and support Depok City's efforts toward Indonesia's national net-zero emissions target for 2060.
